version.message: Update KIP status and KAFKA-21031 repair

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: [DISCUSS] KIP-1371: Explicit Wait Conditions for Consumer Request Managers

JIRA: KAFKA-20995

Release: TBD

Summary

The async consumer has repeatedly entered busy loops when a timer reaches zero while another state blocks the related work. The current numeric wait says when to poll again, but it cannot say whether time can make the work eligible or another event must occur first. Existing fixes replace the zero with another duration, which can make correctness depend on that duration's configuration.

This KIP introduces the internal ManagerPollCondition type with ready(), after(...), and idle(). Each request-manager poll() returns its outgoing requests and the condition for the next manager pass. The same manager decision can govern request admission and network scheduling. The network thread combines all manager conditions and applies the existing network-poll bounds. Public APIs, protocols, and thread topology remain unchanged. The internal per-manager RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long) method becomes applicationPollCondition(long); the application-facing ApplicationEventHandler.maximumTimeToWait() path remains unchanged.

Motivation

The async consumer has repeatedly entered a busy loop when a timer reaches zero while another state prevents the related work from continuing. The loop polls the same request managers, gets the same zero wait, and immediately starts again.

Today, each request manager returns outgoing requests and one numeric wait. The network thread uses the minimum:

java

0 starts another iteration immediately, a finite value schedules a timed iteration, and Long.MAX_VALUE adds no earlier deadline.

The application wait follows the same numeric model. Each manager returns a duration from RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long). The network thread publishes the minimum as cachedMaximumTimeToWait, and the application thread uses it to limit its wait.

Evidence from existing busy-loop fixes

The following issues share the same pattern: work is blocked, but its timer still contributes zero.

EvidenceStatus as of 2026-09-21Affected waitWork blocked bySource of zeroLocal repair
PR #22836 — KAFKA-20253: Heartbeat CPU spin fix for Consumer protocolMergedNetwork scheduling for in-flight coordinator discovery; application wait for heartbeat and auto-commit.Coordinator discovery or heartbeat progress is waiting on coordinator/request state.An elapsed retry or heartbeat timer remains urgent while the related operation cannot advance.Withdraw the in-flight coordinator deadline; use heartbeat or auto-commit intervals on affected application-wait paths.
PR #23227 — KAFKA-20970: Another busy loop happens if auto.commit.interval.ms is less than bootstrap.resolve.timeout.ms MergedApplication waitAuto-commit is waiting for coordinator discovery during bootstrap DNS resolution.The auto-commit timer has expired, so the application wait remains zero.Use the auto-commit interval while the coordinator is unavailable; apply a similar heartbeat-interval guard to Streams.
PR #23348 — KAFKA-21010: Another busy loop happens if the member is in JOINING state and bootstrap DNS resolution is not finishedMergedApplication waitHeartbeat is waiting for coordinator discovery.The initial heartbeat interval is zero while the coordinator remains unknown.Replace zero-capable heartbeat and auto-commit interval substitutes with the retry backoff and refine terminal-state guards.
PR #23357 — KAFKA-21031: Another busy loop happens while a heartbeat is in flight and the heartbeat timer is expiredOpenNetwork scheduling and application waitA heartbeat response is still in flight.The expired heartbeat timer contributes zero even though another heartbeat cannot be sent.Use the configured retry backoff while the heartbeat request is in flight.

Why the current timeout substitutions are incomplete

The fixes repair their reported paths by replacing one zero wait with another duration. PR #22836 and PR #23227 used heartbeat or auto-commit intervals. PR #23348 later used retry backoff because the heartbeat interval starts at zero and auto-commit may be configured as zero. PR #23357 also uses the configured retry backoff while a heartbeat request is in flight.

This approach has three drawbacks:

  • Correctness becomes configuration-dependent. A setting intended to control retry timing also decides whether blocked work enters a busy loop; configuring the replacement timer as zero restores the zero-wait loop.
  • A positive delay only postpones the next poll. Some prerequisites change when an event arrives: a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout resolves an in-flight request, while discovery supplies an unavailable coordinator. If none of these events has occurred, the next poll finds the manager still blocked.
  • A duration does not explain why the manager should run again. When backoff expires, the manager may send a request. When a request is in flight, the same elapsed time changes nothing; the manager still needs a response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout.

The fixes remain correct for their reported cases, but they do not define one rule for future request-manager states.

Public Interfaces

Public consumer classes, metrics, configuration, wire protocols, persisted data, and broker behavior remain unchanged. ManagerPollCondition and the changes to PollResult remain internal to org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.internals.

Proposed Changes

1. Introduce ManagerPollCondition

This KIP introduces the following internal type for request-manager scheduling:

java

The three factories describe when another manager pass can be useful:

FormMeaningWait returned by remainingMs(...)
ready()Another pass can perform work immediately.Zero
after(now, delayMs)Time can make another pass useful.Time remaining to the retained deadline
idle()This work has no local deadline.Long.MAX_VALUE

The implementation represents ready() and idle() as enum singletons:

java

either(first, second) is ready when either input is ready and retains the earlier wait. Therefore, either(ready(), x) is ready(), either(idle(), x) is x, and two timed conditions retain the earlier deadline instance. The implementation may return that instance directly to avoid allocating a composite.

after(...) rejects negative delays and retains one saturating absolute deadline. Zero delay is valid.

isReady(...) authorizes only the action whose condition was checked. A combined condition may be ready because another action expired while request sending remains blocked.

idle() removes only the deadline for this work. Other manager work, independent deadlines, network completions, application events, cancellation, and shutdown can still start another pass. For example, an in-flight heartbeat includes an idle() send condition and its independent max.poll.interval.ms expiry through either(...).

2. A request manager selects and returns its next poll condition

For the condition returned in PollResult, a request manager first checks whether its work can proceed:

text idle() work can proceed now -> ready() time can make the work eligible -> after(now, delayMs)]]>

For request sources using RequestState, one method supplies both request admission and network scheduling:

java

A manager checks sendCondition(now).isReady(now) before creating a request. When no request is created, it returns that condition. After a send, onSendAttempt(...) changes the condition to idle() until a response or failure clears the in-flight state.

Each call to RequestManager.poll(now) answers two questions:

  1. What requests did this manager create in this pass?
  2. When can polling this manager again be useful?

PollResult carries both answers:

java unsentRequests; ManagerPollCondition nextPollCondition; }]]>

The condition describes the manager state after producing the requests. For example, after a request is created and marked in flight, its next condition is normally idle() until the network response changes that state.

3. Apply the rule to current request managers

Manager stateReturned condition
A request is in flight.idle() for sending; keep independent operation expiry with either(...).
Retry backoff remains.after(now, remainingBackoffMs)
Local work can proceed now.ready()
Several requests have different deadlines.Combine their conditions with either(...).

Coordinator discovery, offset commit, topic metadata, and share acknowledgements use RequestState.sendCondition(...). Heartbeat managers use the same rule with their membership state, heartbeat interval, and independent max.poll.interval.ms expiry. Fetch, queued offset work, and membership transitions derive their condition from their existing pending future, queue, or local state.

Correctness still depends on each manager choosing the condition that matches its state. A wrong ready(), a missing prerequisite, or an expired operation left in the manager can still cause repeated immediate passes. Focused tests cover these state transitions.

Evidence from the existing busy-loop fixes

The condition changes below apply to network scheduling. The application-wait repairs in PR #23227, PR #23348, and the application-wait part of PR #23357 keep their existing behavior and remain outside this KIP's scheduling change.

Existing caseCurrent repairCondition returned for network schedulingEffect of the proposed model
PR #22836 — coordinator discovery is in flightRemove the coordinator manager's zero deadline while discovery is pending.idle() until the discovery response, disconnect, cancellation, or timeout changes the state.The manager states directly that time alone cannot enable another discovery request.
PR #23357 — heartbeat is in flight after its timer expiresSubstitute the configured retry backoff.either(idle(), pollExpiryCondition); the send path waits for completion while max.poll.interval.ms remains active.Heartbeat sending no longer depends on a configured substitute timer, and the independent poll expiry is preserved.
PR #23227, PR #23348, and the application-wait part of PR #23357Substitute auto-commit, heartbeat, or retry durations.No change in this KIP.These fixes demonstrate the same duration-substitution pattern; changing application waiting requires separate work.

4. The network thread combines manager results

The following abridged runOnce() shows the scheduling change. The loop keeps the existing manager order and polls each manager once:

java

When one manager makes another manager urgent, it returns ready() to request the next ordered pass. The loop does not poll managers repeatedly within the same pass.

The existing network client poll bounds remain unchanged. This KIP adds no request-timeout query.

Application-thread waiting remains a separate query. The per-manager RequestManager.maximumTimeToWait(long) method becomes applicationPollCondition(long) and returns ManagerPollCondition. The network thread converts those conditions to durations, stores their minimum in cachedMaximumTimeToWait, and keeps the existing ApplicationEventHandler.maximumTimeToWait() path.

Close and drain paths use the remaining request-only PollResult constructors. Their enclosing manager supplies the final condition before returning from poll(...). pollOnClose(long) remains unconditional.

For network scheduling, the proposal changes the three failure points described in Motivation:

Current problemProposed behavior
A replacement timer may be configured as zero and restore the busy loop.Blocked work returns idle() for every timer configuration.
A positive delay schedules another poll even though the manager needs an event.Blocked work returns idle() instead of a deadline. Existing response, disconnect, cancellation, timeout, or discovery processing updates the state and wakes the loop.
A duration alone cannot say whether time can enable the work.ready(), after(...), and idle() state whether work is ready, time can enable it, or time provides no deadline. The manager retains the exact prerequisite in its state.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

The scope is the shared consumer network loop and request managers used by regular, share, and Streams consumers. ClassicKafkaConsumer keeps its existing execution model. Runtime thread names, metrics, application-wait behavior, configuration, protocols, and public consumer APIs remain unchanged.

Every request manager returns ManagerPollCondition in PollResult. Manager order, retry rules, operation deadlines, close behavior, and existing wakeups remain unchanged. A manager may return ready() after a state transition to request the next ordered pass.

Test Plan

  • Condition tests verify ready(), after(...), idle(), either(...), deadline expiry, zero delay, and overflow.
  • Request-manager tests verify that request admission and the returned condition agree for in-flight, backoff, missing-coordinator, independent-expiry, completion, and close states. A blocked manager must resume when its required input arrives.
  • Network-loop tests verify one poll per manager, earliest-deadline selection, the existing network-client request-timeout bounds, and the existing application-wait and close behavior. Integration tests exercise the same paths with real network inputs.
  • Performance tests will compare active throughput and idle CPU against a fixed baseline and require no material regression.

Documentation Plan

Internal Javadocs will define each condition, composition rules, deadline handling, and the difference between network and application waiting. Examples will show one manager decision shared by request admission and scheduling, plus an independent expiry.

Rejected Alternatives

Retain the duration-only request-manager model

Request managers can continue returning a scalar duration and repair each busy loop with local guards or a substitute timeout. The related application-wait fixes and PR #23357 use heartbeat, auto-commit, or retry durations that may themselves be configured as zero. Their configured values then control blocked-state polling even though passage of those durations cannot satisfy the blocking prerequisite.

The proposal retains deadline-driven network polling while replacing the duration-only manager result with explicit conditions. For network scheduling, blocked work uses idle() for every timer configuration; eligible work uses ready() or after(...); independent deadlines combine through either(...). The existing application-wait policy remains unchanged.

results.title: KIP-1372: Reject topic configurations where min.insync.replicas exceeds the replication factor

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: here [Change the link from the KIP proposal email archive to your own email thread]

JIRA: here

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

Kafka currently accepts any min.insync.replicas value of 1 or more, with no relation to the replication factor of the topics it applies to. A topic can be created with --replication-factor 1 --config min.insync.replicas=2 and the request succeeds, even though the configuration is contradictory: the topic can never have enough in-sync replicas to satisfy the configured minimum.

This misconfiguration is not hypothetical. It has been reported since 2017 (KAFKA-4680), where producing with acks=all to such a topic fails with the retriable NotEnoughReplicasException (retries that can never succeed), and the resulting error-log flood filled a broker's disk in a production cluster. Replication tooling that creates topics on a destination cluster whose default min.insync.replicas exceeds the source topic's replication factor hits the same trap, and the failure surfaces far from its cause.

KIP-966 (Eligible Leader Replicas) has already settled the semantic question: the effective minimum ISR of a partition is defined as min(min.insync.replicas, replication factor), and both the controller and the broker silently clamp to that value (ReplicationControlManager#getTopicEffectiveMinIsr, Partition#effectiveMinIsr). In other words, a min.insync.replicas above the replication factor already has no effect: the configured value is simply ignored beyond the clamp. Accepting a value the cluster will never honor is a silent footgun: the user believes they have configured a durability guarantee that does not exist.

This KIP proposes to reject such configurations at the API boundary, where the mistake is made: topic creation and topic-level configuration changes.

Public Interfaces

No new configurations, request/response schema fields, error codes, or APIs are introduced. The change is new validation behavior on two existing request types, using the existing INVALID_CONFIG (40) error code:

APIScenarioCurrent behaviorProposed behavior
CreateTopicsThe topic's resolved replication factor is lower than its effective min.insync.replicasTopic is created; the configured min ISR is silently clamped to the replication factorRequest fails with INVALID_CONFIG
IncrementalAlterConfigs / AlterConfigs (TOPIC resource)min.insync.replicas is set to a value higher than the topic's replication factorChange is accepted and silently clampedRequest fails with INVALID_CONFIG
CreatePartitions, AlterPartitionReassignments, broker-, cluster-, and controller-level configuration changesn/an/aUnchanged (see Proposed Changes for rationale)

For CreateTopics, the resolved replication factor is the request's value, the size of the manual replica assignment if one is given, or the cluster default (default.replication.factor) when the request passes -1. The effective min.insync.replicas is the value that would govern the new topic: the topic-level override in the request if present, otherwise the cluster-level dynamic default, otherwise the static broker/controller configuration.
Example error messages:


Proposed Changes

Validation at topic creation

In the KRaft controller (ReplicationControlManager#createTopic), after the replication factor has been resolved (from the request, the manual assignment, or the cluster default) and before any records are generated, the controller computes the effective min.insync.replicas for the new topic and rejects the creation with INVALID_CONFIG if it exceeds the replication factor.

The check must live here rather than in the existing topic-config validation path (ControllerConfigurationValidator / LogConfig.validate), because that path runs before the replication factor is resolved and receives only the topic name; the replication factor is structurally unavailable to it.

Internal topics (__consumer_offsets, __transaction_state, the share-group and remote-log-metadata state topics) are created through the same path and are validated identically. A rejection there can only occur when the broker's own settings are contradictory (e.g. offsets.topic.replication.factor below the cluster's min.insync.replicas); failing the creation with a clear message surfaces that operator misconfiguration instead of leaving an internal topic that cannot accept acks=all writes. Internal topic creation is retried by brokers, so fixing the configuration heals the cluster without manual intervention.

Validation at topic-level configuration changes

In the controller's configuration handling (ConfigurationControlManager, alongside the ELR-related min.insync.replicas checks introduced by KIP-966), a SET or legacy-alter of min.insync.replicas on a TOPIC resource is rejected with INVALID_CONFIG when the new value exceeds the topic's current replication factor. Both IncrementalAlterConfigs and the deprecated AlterConfigs funnel through the same validation and are covered.

A DELETE of a topic-level min.insync.replicas override remains allowed, even when the topic then falls back to a cluster-level or static default that exceeds its replication factor. The fallback value is not chosen by the caller, and rejecting the delete would prevent returning a topic to defaults; a topic in that state is governed by the effective min ISR clamp, like other grandfathered configurations. (APPEND and SUBTRACT do not arise, since min.insync.replicas is not a list-type config.)

What is deliberately not validated

  • Existing topics are grandfathered. No existing topic is touched, invalidated, or mutated by this KIP. Topics that already carry min.insync.replicas above their replication factor continue to work exactly as today, governed by the KIP-966 clamp. Only new requests that would create or change into a contradictory state are rejected.
  • Deletes of topic-level min.insync.replicas overrides, which fall back to a default that may exceed the replication factor. See "Validation at topic-level configuration changes" above for the rationale.
  • Cluster-level min.insync.replicas changes. Raising the cluster-wide default may put existing low-replication topics above the threshold, but validating it would require scanning every topic on the controller and would block a legitimate operation (hardening the default for future topics). Existing topics remain protected by the clamp; the recommended operator workflow is unchanged.
  • Partition reassignments that lower the replication factor below a topic's min.insync.replicas. Reassignment is an operator-driven surface with its own safeguard (allowReplicationFactorChange, KIP-860), and the clamp keeps the partition writable throughout. Extending validation there can be a follow-up if the community wants it.

Upgrade behavior

The validation is request-time logic on the active controller and requires no new metadata records, so it is not gated on a metadata version or feature flag. In a cluster with mixed controller versions during a rolling upgrade, enforcement begins when an upgraded controller becomes active.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

This is a backward-incompatible behavior change by design: requests that previously succeeded (and produced a configuration the cluster silently ignores) will now fail. We believe the break is acceptable because:

  1. The rejected configurations have no effect today: since KIP-966 the effective min ISR is clamped to the replication factor, no working setup can depend on the accepted-but-ignored value.
  2. The failure is immediate, at the API call that introduces the contradiction, with a message naming both values, as opposed to today's failure modes (producer retry storms, silent clamping) that surface later and elsewhere.
  3. There is precedent for tightening configuration constraints in a major/minor release when the old values were harmful (e.g. KIP-1030).

One workflow requires reordering: increasing durability on an existing topic by setting min.insync.replicas above the current replication factor before adding replicas. After this KIP, the replication factor must be increased first (via reassignment), then min.insync.replicas. Topic-creation workflows are unaffected as long as the requested configuration is self-consistent.

Known deployment patterns affected:

  • Kafka Connect accepts topic-level settings for its internal topics (for example config.storage.min.insync.replicas together with config.storage.replication.factor=-1 to use the broker default; likewise for the offset and status topics, and for source-connector auto-created topics via topic.creation.<alias>.*). Where the resulting min.insync.replicas exceeds the resolved replication factor, internal-topic creation now fails at worker startup with an explicit error, instead of silently creating a topic with a weaker guarantee than the one requested. The remedy is to make the two settings consistent.
  • MirrorMaker 2 is unaffected in its default configuration: min.insync.replicas is on the default config.properties.exclude list and is not synced to mirror topics. Deployments that override the exclude list to sync min.insync.replicas can hit the new validation when the source topic's value exceeds the mirror topic's replication factor.

No deprecation or migration tooling is needed: nothing is removed, and existing topics, including already-contradictory ones, are untouched. Lowering a topic's replication factor is not blocked, so any grandfathered topic can still be repaired in either direction (raise RF or lower min ISR).

Test Plan

Unit tests in ReplicationControlManagerTest and ConfigurationControlManagerTest covering: creation with explicit, defaulted, and manually-assigned replication factors against topic-level, cluster-level, and static min ISR sources; topic-level alteration above/at/below the replication factor; and legacy AlterConfigs. The existing test asserting that a topic with min.insync.replicas above its replication factor is accepted (testEligibleLeaderReplicas_EffectiveMinIsr) will be updated accordingly. Integration coverage is added to the existing CreateTopics/AlterConfigs admin-client tests.

Documentation Plan

The min.insync.replicas description in the topic and broker configuration reference will state the new constraint, and the release's upgrade notes will call out the behavior change.

Rejected Alternatives

  • Throw a new non-retriable exception at produce time (KIP-579's approach). This was the direction proposed in 2020 for KAFKA-4680: keep the configuration legal but fail acks=all produces with a dedicated InconsistentReplicaConfigurationException. It only fires once the data path is exercised: the misconfiguration is accepted and discovered later, by a different principal than the one who made it. It also predates KIP-966, which has since made the configuration semantically void rather than "legal but dangerous". Rejecting at configuration time is strictly earlier and clearer. (KIP-579 itself rejected configuration-time validation partly because such topics were usable with acks!=all; the KIP-966 clamp has since removed any behavior that depended on the un-clamped value, which is why this KIP revisits that conclusion.)
  • Introduce a new error code (KIP-579 had reserved INCONSISTENT_REPLICA_CONFIGURATION(89); that code has since been assigned to THROTTLING_QUOTA_EXCEEDED). Clients that don't know a new code surface it as UnknownServerException. INVALID_CONFIG is already returned by both affected APIs for other invalid topic configurations, is handled by every client version, and describes the problem accurately.
  • Validate cluster-level min.insync.replicas changes against all existing topics. Requires an O(topics) scan on the controller for a dynamic-config update, and would block hardening the default for future topics just because legacy low-replication topics exist. The clamp already protects existing topics.
  • Rely on CreateTopicPolicy/AlterConfigPolicy (KIP-108/KIP-133). Operators can enforce this today with a custom policy, but policies are opt-in, must be deployed on every cluster, and don't help the users who hit this by accident, which is exactly the population this KIP is for. A contradiction between two settings of the same topic is a consistency rule, not a site policy.
  • Documentation-only fix. The constraint has been documented in the min.insync.replicas description for years; KAFKA-4680-style incidents kept occurring regardless.

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

Brokers already expose per-client quota usage byte-rate , request-time  and throttle time throttle-time . They do not expose how that usage compares to the effective quota applied to the same quota sensor.

That join is left to operators: scrape the rate, then independently resolve user, client-id, and default overrides (or a custom ClientQuotaCallback)  from a different path. Limits can differ by orders of magnitude and can change dynamically, so absolute-rate alerts do not transfer across clients.

throttle-time  only changes after throttling has occurred. Operators need a normalized rate signal that identifies clients whose recent usage is approaching or exceeding the quota actually applied on that broker, without requiring the monitoring stack to resolve the quota independently.

KIP-1257: Partition Size Percentage Metrics for Storage Monitoring established the precedent of shipping a normalized percentage from Kafka rather than requiring operators to compute it externally. The analogy is only partial: retention.bytes  is a topic configuration, while client quotas are resolved per quota entity through the existing quota hierarchy and optional callbacks. This KIP preserves the existing quota-resolution and enforcement behavior.

Proposed Changes

Add quota-utilization as an additional attribute on the existing client-quota MBeans. No new MBean type, ObjectName, sensor, or quota entity is introduced.   

existingnew
byte-rate | request-time ,  throttle-timequota-utilization

Definition

quota-utilization is the recent quota-measured rate expressed as a percentage of the effective quota applied to the same quota sensor.

calculation
  • Measured rate is the value of the existing quota rate metric on that sensor (byte-rate or request-time).
  • Effective quota is the quota currently associated with that rate metric's MetricConfig, after callback resolution and default/override resolution, and is the same bound used for enforcement on that sensor.
  • The metric is a rate-utilization signal. It is not a representation of throttle state or of remaining headroom before the next request is delayed.

Value and meaning

  • Less than 100: recent rate is below the effective quota.
  • Equal to 100: recent rate equals the effective quota.
  • Greater than 100: recent rate exceeds the effective quota; not capped.

throttle-time: actual throttling that already occurred.

The result is always a percentage of the applicable quota, regardless of the physical unit of the numerator.

Quotanumeratordenominator
Producebyte-rate (bytes/sec)producer_byte_rate
Fetchbyte-rate (bytes/sec)consumer_byte_rate
Requestrequest-timerequest_percentage

Request units are the easiest to misread. request-time is already a percentage of broker network and I/O thread time, and request_percentage caps that quantity. Utilization is a percentage of that cap, not request-time / 100. Exempt request time is not included in the numerator.

Examples

QuotaInputQuota-utilization
Producebyte-rate = 800 KiB/s, producer_byte_rate = 1 MiB/s80
Requestrequest-time = 40, request_percentage = 5080 (40 percent of the pool, 80 percent of the client quota)
Unlimitedbyte-rate = 800 KiB/s, quota = Long.MaxValueNaN

Effective quota

The denominator is not re-resolved by calling ClientQuotaCallback.quotaLimit() during metric collection.

Kafka already writes the resolved bound onto the quota rate metric when the sensor is created and when quota configuration is updated (MetricConfig.quota). Utilization uses that cached bound.

Consequences:

  • JMX and reporter scrapes do not execute custom callback code.
  • ClientQuotaCallback invocation frequency is unchanged.
  • If a custom callback changes limits only through the existing update paths (updateQuota, or quotaResetRequired triggering a metric config refresh), utilization stays aligned with enforcement.

This KIP does not add a requirement that callbacks be safe to run on the scrape path.

Resolution of user, client-id, and default quotas is unchanged. It follows the existing documented client-quota precedence; this KIP does not restate or alter that hierarchy.

A missing, non-positive, or unlimited bound (greater than or equal to Long.MaxValue, Kafka's unlimited sentinel) is not a meaningful denominator, and yields NaN.

Scope

Produce, Fetch, and Request quotas are enforced independently on each broker. The metric on broker A is the client's usage on broker A divided by the quota applied on broker A. It is not cluster-wide quota headroom.

Operators should therefore scrape every broker and should not average the metric across brokers and interpret the result as cluster-wide utilization.

Controller Mutation

ControllerMutation quotas are not included in version 1.

Controller mutation quotas are enforced using a token bucket (tokens), while this KIP defines quota-utilization as a windowed rate divided by the configured rate. A windowed mutation-rate ratio would therefore not represent how much of the resource that actually controls throttling is currently available.

For example, a burst can exhaust tokens and cause throttle-time while the windowed mutation rate is still below 100%. Conversely, the windowed mutation rate can remain above 100% after the token bucket has begun to refill.

A future KIP can define an appropriate ControllerMutation metric, either as explicit rate utilization or as a token-bucket/remaining-token metric.

This KIP does not cover:

  • Replica and replication quotas LeaderReplication, FollowerReplication, AlterLogDirsReplication
  • Remote-log copy or fetch quotas
  • Connection-rate quotas
  • Max-connections quotas

These quotas use different managers, units, or MBeans and can be addressed separately.

Presence, NaN, and sensor lifecycle

The attribute is present exactly when the existing quota sensor exists. Presence is not a function of whether the current bound is finite.

That distinguishes the following cases:

  • Finite quota, from an override or a matching default: sensor and attribute are present; value is measured-rate / effective-quota * 100.
  • Quotas of this type never configured (quotasEnabled == false): sensor and attribute are absent, same as byte-rate today.
  • Sensor exists, bound is unlimited, missing, or non-positive: sensor and attribute are present; value is NaN.
  • Quotas configured, then all removed, quotasEnabled becomes false immediately. Sensors created before removal remain until the existing inactive-sensor expiry; quota-utilization is NaN because the bound is the unlimited sentinel. New sensors are not created until a quota is configured again.
  • Inactive client, sensor expired after the existing one hour expiry: sensor and attribute are absent until traffic resumes.

NaN means there is no finite quota to divide by. It does not mean 0 percent used. The attribute is kept on the MBean so that "sensor exists, no finite denominator" stays distinguishable from "quotas were never enabled, no MBean". Returning 0 for an unlimited quota would look like an idle, well-behaved client.

The metric is a double, as the neighbouring attributes already are. Exporter handling of JMX NaN is implementation dependent, so operators should verify their collector. Aggregations that require finite input should exclude NaN samples.

Fetch may unrecord bytes that were not returned after throttling. Utilization can therefore fall back below 100 percent on the same request that recorded throttle-time. This is existing rate-metric behaviour rather than something introduced here. Produce does not unrecord.

Public Interfaces

JMX

QuotaProduced onMBeanAttributes after this KIP
​Produce​Every broker​kafka.server:type=Produce,user=...,client-id=...​byte-rate, throttle-time, quota-utilization
FetchEvery brokerkafka.server:type=Fetch,user=...,client-id=...​byte-rate, throttle-time, quota-utilization
RequestEvery brokerkafka.server:type=Request,user=...,client-id=...​request-time, throttle-time, quota-utilization

There are no new broker configurations, request APIs, or Admin APIs.

Tags

quota-utilization uses exactly the same metric tags as the existing quota rate metric.

With the default quota callback, these are user and client-id. Either tag may be empty:

  • Per-client-id quotas have an empty user tag.
  • Per-user quotas have an empty client-id tag.
  • User plus client-id quotas have both tags populated.

A custom ClientQuotaCallback may provide additional metric tags. quota-utilization uses those same tags and does not introduce a second tag namespace.

The metric is an additional attribute on the same sensor and ObjectName as byte-rate or request-time.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

  • The change is additive: an attribute is added to existing MBeans.
  • Existing MBean ObjectNames are unchanged.
  • Scrapers that ignore unknown attributes continue to work.
  • Scrapers that allowlist attributes by name must add quota-utilization to collect the new metric.
  • ClientQuotaCallback behavior and invocation frequency are unchanged.
  • Metric collection does not invoke ClientQuotaCallback.quotaLimit().
  • There are no deprecations.
  • There is no protocol migration.
  • After upgrade, the attribute appears when the existing quota sensor is created, which occurs on the first recorded traffic after quotas have been enabled for that quota type.

Proposed Implementation

The implementation adds a MeasurableStat named quota-utilization when the existing quota sensor is registered.

At measurement time, the stat uses:

  • The existing quota rate measurement as the numerator.
  • The quota associated with the same metric's MetricConfig as the denominator.
  • Double.NaN when the denominator is missing, non-positive, or unlimited.

Dynamic quota updates already refresh the quota metric configuration. No additional quota-resolution path is introduced.

The request path does not resolve quotas again, does not change enforcement, and does not add a second accumulating rate. Utilization is a no-op MeasurableStat on the existing quota sensor, so Sensor.record invokes one extra empty record().

Test Plan

The Apache Kafka PR will include tests covering at least the following:

  • Produce: utilization equals byte-rate / quota * 100.
  • Fetch: utilization equals byte-rate / quota * 100.
  • Request: utilization equals request-time / request_percentage * 100.
  • Default, user, and user-plus-client-id quota tags match the existing rate metric.
  • Unlimited, missing, and non-positive bounds produce NaN.
  • Finite-to-unlimited quota updates produce NaN after the metric configuration is refreshed.
  • Values greater than 100 are preserved and are not capped.
  • Fetch unrecord behavior is reflected in the resulting utilization.
  • JMX exposes quota-utilization as a double attribute on the existing quota MBeans.
  • The measure path does not invoke ClientQuotaCallback.quotaLimit.

Rejected Alternatives

AlternativeReason
Computing utilization in the monitoring stackOperators could divide the existing usage metric by the configured quota externally. This requires independently resolving defaults, overrides, dynamic updates, and custom ClientQuotaCallback behavior. The broker already has the effective quota associated with the quota metric, so computing utilization in the broker avoids duplicating that logic.
Adding a new MBean or metric namespaceA new MBean or metric namespace would add unnecessary complexity and cardinality. quota-utilization is an additional attribute on the existing quota MBeans, keeping the metric alongside the usage and throttling metrics it complements.
Using a PascalCase metric name such as QuotaUtilizationPercentThe existing client quota metrics use kebab-case names such as byte-rate, request-time, and throttle-time. quota-utilization follows the existing naming convention and makes the denominator explicit.
Integer percentagesThe existing quota MBean attributes are double values. Returning a floating-point percentage preserves useful resolution around common alerting thresholds such as 70%, 80%, and 90%.
Returning 0 for unlimited quotas0 could be interpreted as zero usage or an idle client. NaN makes it explicit that no meaningful percentage can be calculated because there is no finite quota.
Omitting the attribute for unlimited quotasThe attribute follows the lifecycle of the existing quota sensor. Keeping it present and returning NaN distinguishes an existing quota sensor with no finite denominator from a sensor that does not exist because quotas were never enabled.
Capping utilization at 100%The measured rate can temporarily exceed the configured quota. Values above 100% provide useful information about rate overshoot and should not be capped.
Broker-level aggregated utilizationProduce, Fetch, and Request quotas are enforced independently on each broker. Aggregating utilization across brokers can hide the broker where a client is approaching its quota. Aggregation is left to the monitoring system based on the operator's alerting intent.
Including ControllerMutation quotasControllerMutation quotas use token-bucket enforcement rather than the windowed rate model used by Produce, Fetch, and Request. A windowed rate percentage would therefore not represent token-bucket headroom or reliably predict throttling. ControllerMutation can be addressed separately with a metric whose semantics match its enforcement model.
Exposing a separate quota-limit metricA quota-limit metric could be useful, particularly for idle or unlimited clients, but is not required for the primary use case of normalized utilization alerting. It can be considered as a follow-up.
Calling quotaLimit() during metric collectionResolving the quota through ClientQuotaCallback.quotaLimit() on every metric scrape would change the callback contract and could execute custom callback code as a result of JMX or metrics collection. The effective quota is already associated with the quota metric through MetricConfig, so utilization uses that value instead.
Time-to-throttle or remaining-headroom metricsThese metrics require assumptions about future client behavior and can be misleading. quota-utilization reports the recent measured rate relative to the effective quota, while throttle-time remains the signal for actual throttling.

StreamsBuilder.globalTable()  currently lags behind the functionality of StreamsBuilder.addGlobalStore() which lets users rekey data from a topic before populating the GlobalStateStore.  StreamsBuilder.globalTable  currently does not  let a client remap keys when building a GlobalKTable  from a topic. This KIP introduces 4 new overloads to globalTable  that lets clients remap keys when building a GlobalKTable . The current overrides of globalTable  source their GlobalKTable  with an internal KTableSource  . KTableSource  provides no callback to remap keys so we will create the following new internal classes.


java implements ProcessorSupplier> { private class KTableSourceWithRemappingProcessor implements Processor> }]]>


The behavior of these classes is similar to the existing KTableSource  and KTableSourceProcessor  classes. The difference is that a KeyValueMapper  is run at the start of KTableSourceWithRemappingProcessor.process. The mapper is a data member of KTableSourceWithRemapping  and is injectable via a constructor.


To avoid code duplication, the implementation of KTableSource  will be changed to compose a dlegate KTableSourceWithRemapping with an identity KeyValueMapper which it will delegate its logic to. KTableSourceProcessor will be deleted.


The table semantics of converting values to Change<V>  objects will be now owned by KTableSourceWithRemappingProcessor  instead of KTableSourceProcessor .




Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan


This change is fully backwards compatable. Existing users should not be affected. No externally facing classes, methods, or interfaces will be deleted. The internals of the existing globalTable  methods will be changed but this should not be observable by a Kafka user.


Test Plan


We will add unit tests for the "WithRemapping"  classes and integration tests for the new overrides of globalTable. We will use existing unit and integration tests to confirm there are no regressions in the behavior KTableSource  and the existing globalTable  overrides.

We may need to add more unit and integration tests for the existing components to cover scenarios that may differ when run through a unit remapper (i.g. null keys).

Rejected Alternatives

Use a ProcessorSupplier instead of a KeyValueMapper as an argument for globalTable


This would let a user supply a ProcessorSupplier  instead of a KeyValueMapper, letting them perform arbitrary stateless processing steps from the topic instead of just remapping. The problem is that a GlobalStateStore  is associated with only one state updater ProcessorSupplier . KTableSource is the currently used as the processor supplier, but letting a user inject their own processor supplier means that the user must have their ProcessorSupplier  implement table semantics. Using a KeyValueMapper abstracts the table semantics change away from the user. Changing GlobalStateStore  to use more than one ProcessorSupplier  to update its state seems like a nontrivial change that may have unforseen consequences.

Status

Discussion thread: here (not made yet)

JIRA: here

Motivation


The interface StateRestoreListener has a method onRestoreSuspended  which lets a client observe the restoration of a StateStore  when that StateStore's restoration is suspended before it is finished.

StateRestoreListener.onRestoreSuspended  currently does not provide the reason for the restoration being suspended. The suspension can happen for one of three reasons:


  • the task was assigned to another instance
  • the task was demoted to a standby task on this instance
  • the instance is shutting down


A StateRestoreListener  is currently unable to differentiate between these reasons even though these reasons may be useful for a Kafka user who, for example, wants to emit observability to diagnose their application.


The analagous listener for standby tasks StateUpdateListener does provide the suspension reason for its analagous method, StateUpdateListener.onUpdateSuspended . Adding the suspension reason to the StateRestoreListener 

would fix this mismatch in the listener API.

Public Interfaces

Briefly list any new interfaces that will be introduced as part of this proposal or any existing interfaces that will be removed or changed. The purpose of this section is to concisely call out the public contract that will come along with this feature.

A public interface is any change to the following:

  • Binary log format

  • The network protocol and api behavior

  • Any class in the public packages under clientsConfiguration, especially client configuration

    • org/apache/kafka/common/serialization

    • org/apache/kafka/common

    • org/apache/kafka/common/errors

    • org/apache/kafka/clients/producer

    • org/apache/kafka/clients/consumer (eventually, once stable)

  • Monitoring

  • Command line tools and arguments

  • Anything else that will likely break existing users in some way when they upgrade


Changes to StateUpdateListener


StateUpdateListener  will add a new overload of .onUpdateSuspend  that has the suspension reason as an argument. the old. The new overload will have a default implementation to call the old .onUpdateSuspend  while dropping the suspension reason.

This method is called after restoring each batch and it is advised to keep processing to a minimum. * Any heavy processing will block the state updater thread and hold up recovering the next batch, hence slowing * down the restore process as a whole. * If you need to do any extended processing or connecting to an external service consider doing so asynchronously. * * @param topicPartition * the {@link TopicPartition} containing the values to restore * @param storeName * the name of the store undergoing restoration * @param batchEndOffset * the inclusive ending offset for the current restored batch for this {@link TopicPartition} * @param numRestored * the total number of records restored in this batch for this {@link TopicPartition} */ void onBatchRestored( final TopicPartition topicPartition, final String storeName, final long batchEndOffset, final long numRestored ); /** * Method called when restoring the {@link StateStore} is complete. * * @param topicPartition * the {@link TopicPartition} containing the values to restore * @param storeName * the name of the store just restored * @param totalRestored * the total number of records restored for this {@link TopicPartition} */ void onRestoreEnd( final TopicPartition topicPartition, final String storeName, final long totalRestored ); /** * Method called when restoring the {@link StateStore} is suspended before it finished, because the task stopped * being an active task on this host: it was assigned elsewhere, demoted to a standby task, or this host is shutting * down (the concrete reason is not reported). * If the task becomes an active task on this host again -- assigned back to it, or promoted from the standby task * it was demoted to -- another {@link #onRestoreStart(TopicPartition, String, long, long)} would be called. * *

  • Swap KafkaStreams.DelegatingStateRestoreListener.OnRestoreSuspended  to use the new four argument overload
    • note that DelegatingStateRestoreListener is package private, so this is a backwards compatible change
  • Modify StateChangelogReader.unregister to pass the reason it calculates into its call to StateRestoreListener.OnRestoreSuspended  (effectively replacing the call to existing .OnRestoreSuspended  with a call to its overload

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

Kafka 4.X

The existing method will be deprecated but its observable behavior will remain the same to a caller. Existing implementations of StateRestoreListener  will remain implementations due to the use of a default method.

This ensures that backwards compatibility will remain during 4.X releases.


Kafka 5.0

When Kafka 5.0 releases, we can remove the deprecated original overload of StateRestoreListener.OnRestoreSuspended . This is a backwards breaking change.

Test Plan


  • Unit tests for new method overload
  • Enforce that an implementation that does not explicitly define the new overload of OnRestoresSuspended  is still able to implement StateRestoreListener (likely through an anonymous implementation in a unit test)

Defining a new interface that extends from StateRestoreListener that adds this overload

this was rejected because using a default method for the new overload provided a cleaner way of adding the change without breaking backwards compatability

results.title: KIP-1376: Support setting TLS named groups

storage.value:
Status

Current state: In Discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: KAFKA-20728 

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

Named groups are how the JVM describes TLS key exchange schemes. APIs to use named groups have been added in Java 20.

Via JEP 527: Post-Quantum Hybrid Key Exchange for TLS 1.3, new key exchange schemes resistant to quantum attacks, usually referred to as Post Quantum Cryptography (PQC), are being introduced. This JEP was initially delivered in Java 27. It's being backported by several implementations to earlier Java versions. Note that the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() API is available from Java 20, but the PQC named groups themselves (e.g. x25519_mlkem768) require Java 27 or a vendor backport that includes JEP 527.

Due to threats like "harvest now, decrypt later", many organizations are now actively considering PQC TLS. It is also mandated by several governments and industries such as finance, healthcare and defense.

Public Interfaces

All communication channels that are encrypted via TLS need to support PQC. This includes:

  • Client to broker/controller
  • Broker/controller to client
  • Broker/controller to broker/controller
  • Connect workers accepting REST traffic
  • Connect worker to Connect worker
  • OAuth token retrieval (client)
  • OAuth JWKS retrieval (server)

To cover all these scenarios, a single configuration can be used:
Name: ssl.named.groups
Type: List
Default: Empty, the default JVM named groups are used
Description: An ordered list of key exchange named groups to use for SSL connections, with the most preferred group first. The supported values depend on the SSL provider and Java runtime.

It can be set in clients, servers, Streams instances and Connect worker configurations. For example:


On servers, it can also be set per listener, for example:


For OAuth it must be set via sasl.jaas.config or a JAAS file, for example:


If the configuration is set and the JVM does not support the named groups APIs, a ConfigException will be thrown at startup.
If the configuration is set to unknown named groups, the failure happens when the TLS connection is established. This is the same behavior as with ssl.cipher.suites.
If the configuration is set, like with ssl.cipher.suites, a TLS connection can only be established when the client and server share at least one named group.
The TLS version (set via ssl.protocol) gates what named groups are valid and automatically drops entries not compatible (like for ciphers). 

Proposed Changes

The named groups APIs are only available in Java 20+. Because the Kafka modules still support Java 11 (clients) and Java 17 (servers), logic trying to set named groups will use reflection so it compiles with the currently supported Java versions.

Clients/Servers

The DefaultSslEngineFactory class handles the TLS logic for clients and brokers. If ssl.named.groups is set, the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() method will be called via reflection.

OAuth

The OAuth/OIDC implementation makes two types of outbound HTTPS connections to the identity provider:

  • Token retrieval (client-side): OAuthBearerLoginCallbackHandler uses HttpJwtRetriever to fetch JWT access tokens from the token endpoint. Every Kafka client (producer, consumer, admin) and broker (for inter-broker OAuth) makes this call on each token refresh.
  • JWKS key retrieval (broker-side): OAuthBearerValidatorCallbackHandler uses VerificationKeyResolverFactory to periodically fetch the identity provider's public keys from the JWKS endpoint, which are used to verify JWT signatures.

The JaasOptionsUtils.createSSLSocketFactory() method will be updated to wrap the returned SSLSocketFactory so that SSLParameters (including named groups, cipher suites, and enabled protocols) are applied to each socket after creation, mirroring what DefaultSslEngineFactory does for clients and servers.

Connect REST API

Connect uses Jetty to expose its REST API for users and for worker-to-worker communications.

  • Server-side: This handles REST API traffic from users and other Connect workers.
  • Client-side: This is used to forward requests to other Connect workers.

Both paths go through SSLUtils.configureSslContextFactoryAlgorithms(), which currently configures protocols, cipher suites, SSL provider, and algorithm settings. It will be updated to also set named groups if the configuration is set.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

  • The ssl.named.groups configuration is new and optional. When not set, the JVM's default named groups are used so existing behavior is unchanged.
  • The SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() API is required for this feature. The implementation uses reflection so it compiles with older Java versions. If ssl.named.groups is set when the Java runtime lacks the SSLParameters.setNamedGroups() then a ConfigException is thrown with a clear error message at startup.
  • The ssl.named.groups configuration is not dynamically reconfigurable. Changing it requires a restart. A phased PQC rollout can be achieved via rolling restarts across the cluster.
  • Since Java 8, users can set the jdk.tls.namedGroups system property to set named groups at the JVM level. The table below details the interaction between the system property and the new configuration:
    ssl.named.groupsjdk.tls.namedGroupsBehavior

    not set

    		not setJVM built-in defaults
    not setsetSystem property applies
    setnot setKafka config applies
    setsetKafka config takes precedence:
    If ssl.named.groups is set all connections use the specified named groups.
    If only listener.name.internal.ssl.named.groups is set, the internal listener uses the specified named groups. If there are other listeners, they use the system property if it's set, otherwise the JVM built-in defaults.
    Effectively the precedence chain is:
      1. listener.name.<name>.ssl.named.groups (per-listener override when available)
      2. ssl.named.groups (global Kafka config)
      3. jdk.tls.namedGroups (JVM system property)
      4. JVM built-in defaults

    The behavior is consistent with how the cipher suites work (via ssl.cipher.suites and jdk.tls.client.cipherSuites).

Test Plan

  • Unit tests covering the changes for all components.
  • Integration tests verify end-to-end TLS connections with named groups configured for client-broker, inter-broker, and Connect REST scenarios. 
  • These tests will be skipped when run on a JVM that does not support named groups. The CI already runs with Java 25, so this will be effectively tested.
  • Tests that exercise the error handling in case of lack of support for named groups will run in the CI with Java 17.

Rejected Alternatives

  • Rely on the JVM jdk.tls.namedGroups system property: This property applies to the whole JVM, so it prevents using different named groups for different components/listeners.
  • Distinguish between null and empty for ssl.named.groups: This only enables very niche scenarios (for example resetting named groups for a specific listener). I favored aligning the behavior with the ssl.cipher.suites configuration.
  • Do a multi-release JAR: A multi-release JAR could be used instead of relying on reflection. Overall using reflection is simpler and does not require making build changes.

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

The consumer read path avoids a per-record copy for the record value. KIP-863 added a ByteBuffer method to Deserializer so that CompletedFetch#parseRecord can hand the deserializer the record value straight from the fetch buffer:

javaDeserializer.java


The default falls back to the byte[] method, so existing deserializers are unaffected, and ByteBufferDeserializer overrides it to skip the copy.

The producer has no matching method. Serializer only returns byte[]:

javaSerializer.java

So a producer whose record value is already in a ByteBuffer has to copy it into a byte[] for every record. This is the case for a caller that holds data off the Java heap or in a reused buffer, for example a Netty ByteBuf exposed through nioBuffer(), or a service that forwards a payload it does not read.

This KIP adds the missing method so the write side matches the read side that KIP-863 already added. It is opt-in, so a serializer that returns byte[] keeps working with no change.

Public Interfaces

Serializer.serializeToBuffer

A new default method on org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.Serializer<T>:

javaSerializer.java

A separate name is used because Java cannot overload on the return type alone.

ByteBufferSerializer

org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.ByteBufferSerializer overrides the method to return the buffer without copying:


javaByteBufferSerializer.java

duplicate() gives the producer its own position and limit. The caller's buffer is left unchanged and can be refilled and reused for the next record.

Partitioner.partition with a ByteBuffer key

A new default method on org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner, so that choosing the partition from the key does not force a byte[] copy of the key:

javaPartitioner.java

A custom Partitioner that implements only the byte[] method keeps working. It receives a copied key, the same as today. Only the built-in partitioner skips the copy.

Proposed Changes

KafkaProducer.doSend calls serializeToBuffer in place of serialize. For the default serializers this wraps the byte[] and behaves as before. For ByteBufferSerializer it passes the caller's buffer through with no copy.

The producer already copies the payload into the record batch once, when it writes the record. This only change removes the extra per-record byte[] that the serializer uses to allocate. The producer reads the returned buffer without moving its position, so a caller can hand in the same ByteBuffer on every send and refill it in place.

Currently, Utils#murmur2 hash operates on byte[] array and we would provide bit identical version backed by a ByteBuffer.

All references from MemoryRecordsBuilder -> DefaultRecord operate on ByteBuffers. However, there is an implementation cost associated with the Utils#writeTo method that currently does a array copy directly since the backing store for the ByteBuffer is a byte array. For uncompressed payloads, we can write the ByteBufferDataOutputStream directly into the appendStream of MemoryRecordsBuilder.

Extension Considerations

This method is the serializer step of the send path. It removes the copy where the value enters the producer. It does not by itself, keep the value off the heap all the way to the socket in the current flow. A caller who wants that should know the points where the value still touches the heap today. Each is a separate concern and is not part of this KIP.

  • Batch memory: The producer copies each record into a batch buffer before it is sent, and that buffer is on the heap today. This is the only point that grows with the record size, but can be capped with the batch.size config today. An offheap version of this bufferpool can be a follow-up KIP.
  • Compression: The compression codecs take byte[] input, so a ByteBuffer value is copied through a small heap buffer, reused across records, before it reaches the codec. A ByteBuffer codec input path would be a separate change.
  • TLS: With the built-in JDK TLS provider the plaintext is copied to the heap inside the SSLEngine. Keeping it off-heap through TLS needs a native provider, which is already pluggable through ssl.engine.factory.class. For instance, Netty's SSLEngine provides this capability and users can configure a custom netty SSLEngine Factory.

Of these, only the batch buffer grows with the record size. The compression and TLS buffers are fixed and reused, so are not affected by the payload size.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

serializeToBuffer is a default method, so every existing Serializer compiles and runs unchanged. The new Partitioner.partition overload is also a default method, so existing partitioners are unaffected. A custom partitioner that implements only the byte[] method receives a copied key, the same as today.

There is no wire protocol change, no broker change, and no required configuration. A producer configured with ByteBufferSerializer and passing ByteBuffer values stops allocating a byte[] per record with no application code change.

Test Plan

  • A Serializer that implements only serialize returns the same bytes through the default serializeToBuffer.
  • ByteBufferSerializer.serializeToBuffer returns the data without moving the caller's position, and returns null for a null value.
  • KafkaProducer.doSend produces byte-identical records through the byte[] and ByteBuffer paths, for heap and direct input buffers.
  • The built-in partitioner chooses the same partition for a ByteBuffer key and the equal byte[] key.

Rejected Alternatives

Change the return type of Serializer.serialize, or add a required method. This would break every existing serializer. A default method keeps the change opt-in and source-compatible, the same way KIP-863 added the ByteBuffer deserialize method.

Add the ByteBuffer key method to the Partitioner contract as a required method. Every custom partitioner would have to implement it. The default method keeps them working and copies the key for them, the same as today.

storage.value:
Status

Current state: "Under Discussion"

Discussion thread: DISCUSS: KIP-1378: Allow Consumer Group Renaming in MirrorMaker 2 Checkpoint Connector

JIRA: KAFKA-21127 

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

MirrorMaker 2 (MM2) provides pluggable topic renaming across clusters via the `ReplicationPolicy` interface (e.g., `DefaultReplicationPolicy` prefixes topic names with the source cluster alias `<source>.<topic>`, while `IdentityReplicationPolicy` keeps them identical).

However, consumer groups do not have an equivalent pluggable naming mechanism. Today, `MirrorCheckpointConnector` and `MirrorCheckpointTask` mirror consumer group offsets to the target cluster preserving the exact source consumer group ID (`group.id`).

When multiple primary clusters replicate into a single disaster recovery (DR) or analytical target cluster, consumer group names from different source clusters can easily collide if identical group IDs were used independently on each source.

This KIP proposes introducing a pluggable `GroupMirroringPolicy` interface (analogous to `ReplicationPolicy`) to allow operators to customize consumer group names created and tracked on the target cluster.

Public Interfaces

New Interface: `org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.GroupMirroringPolicy`
```
package org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror;

/**
 * An interface used by MirrorMaker connectors to rename consumer groups between source and target clusters.
 * Analogous to ReplicationPolicy for topics, this allows operators to define a custom naming
 * convention for consumer groups on the target cluster.
 */
@InterfaceAudience.Public
public interface GroupMirroringPolicy extends Configurable {

 /**
 * Returns the name that the given source consumer group should use on the target cluster.
 * This name is used when emitting checkpoints and syncing consumer group offsets to the target.
 *
 * @param sourceClusterAlias the alias of the source cluster
 * @param group the consumer group ID on the source cluster
 * @return the consumer group ID to use on the target cluster
 */
 String targetGroupId(String sourceClusterAlias, String group);

 /**
 * Returns the source consumer group ID for a given group on the target cluster.
 * This is the inverse of targetGroupId(String, String).
 *
 * @param sourceClusterAlias the alias of the source cluster
 * @param targetGroup the consumer group ID on the target cluster
 * @return the original consumer group ID on the source cluster, or null if not determinable
 */
 String sourceGroupId(String sourceClusterAlias, String targetGroup);

 @Override
 default void configure(Map<String, ?> configs) {
 // no-op by default
 }
}
```


Default Implementation: `org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.DefaultGroupMirroringPolicy`
An identity implementation providing backward-compatible default behavior:


3. New Configuration Property

The following configuration property is added to `MirrorCheckpointConfig` and `MirrorClientConfig`:


 `group.mirroring.policy.class`

Type: `Class`
Deafult: `org.apache.kafka.connect.mirror.DefaultGroupMirroringPolicy`
Importance : `LOW`
Description: Class which defines the consumer group naming convention on the target cluster.

  • Fully backward compatible. Existing setups without this configuration will use `DefaultGroupMirroringPolicy`, which preserves existing consumer group IDs verbatim.
