Build System Test Dependencies Image workflow

New

Runs on trunk pushes that touch tests/docker/deps/**, or by hand

Proposed Changes

One image, ghcr.io/apache/kafka/system-test-deps, holds every release the system tests need. A workflow builds it from the official artifacts, and the ducker image copies it instead of downloading from S3.

The deps image

A new directory, tests/docker/deps/, holds a Dockerfile and a fetch-kafka.sh script. The Dockerfile lists one line per release:

RUN fetch-kafka 4.2.2 2.13
RUN fetch-kafka 4.3.1 2.13

fetch-kafka.sh <version> <scala version> does the following:

  1. Downloads kafka_<scala>-<version>.tgz from https://archive.apache.org/dist/kafka/<version>/.
  2. Downloads kafka-streams-<version>-test.jar from Maven Central.
  3. Verifies both detached signatures against https://downloads.apache.org/kafka/KEYS, as docker/jvm/Dockerfile already does for the release image.
  4. Installs the release into /opt/kafka-<version> and puts the test jar into its libs/.

The publishing workflow

A new workflow, .github/workflows/system_test_deps_image.yml, builds and pushes the image:

Setting

Value

Why

Trigger

A push to trunk that touches tests/docker/deps/**, or workflow_dispatch

The image is published as soon as the release PR merges

Tags

The git tree hash of tests/docker/deps (12 characters), plus latest from trunk

The hash names the content and never moves; latest follows trunk

Changes to tests/docker/Dockerfile

The curl lines become a stage and one COPY:

ARG KAFKA_DEPS_IMAGE="ghcr.io/apache/kafka/system-test-deps:latest"
FROM $KAFKA_DEPS_IMAGE AS kafka-deps
...
COPY --from=kafka-deps /opt/ /opt/

To build without GHCR, for example offline or with local changes, build the deps image first and pass it in:

docker build -t kafka-system-test-deps tests/docker/deps tests/docker/ducker-ak up --build-arg KAFKA_DEPS_IMAGE=kafka-system-test-deps

Changes to the release process

After a release, the release manager adds or bumps one line in tests/docker/deps/Dockerfile, next to the existing version.py and dependencies.gradle changes. The S3 upload step will be removed from the Release Process, because the workflow publishes the image when that PR merges.

Vagrant

This KIP does not change vagrant/base.sh. It stays as is for now and keeps downloading from the S3 mirror, so it no longer gets new releases once the S3 upload step is removed. Removing Vagrant is tracked in KAFKA-21260.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

No user-facing changes.

Test Plan

The change only moves files, so the main test is that the ducker image ends up with the same /opt as today. The system tests that start older releases should pass.

Rejected Alternatives

  • Let other PMC members push to the S3 bucket. This removes the need to ask a Confluent committer, but the upload stays a manual After release step that can be forgotten, and the copies are still not checked against the release signatures. Access to the bucket would also still be managed by Confluent.
  • Download from archive.apache.org in tests/docker/Dockerfile. Every first build would pull about 2.1 GB from the ASF archive, which throttles heavy users to 12 or 6 Mbps and bans clients that download more than 40 GB a week.
  • Publish the image to Docker Hub. The apache/ namespace there holds the user-facing apache/kafka images, so a test-only image could be mistaken for a release, and Docker Hub rate-limits anonymous pulls.

results.title: KIP-1386: Per-call record limit for Consumer poll

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-21350

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

max.poll.records and max.poll.interval.ms are read when a consumer is constructed and neither can be changed afterwards.

If processing slows down, a batch that used to fit inside the poll interval stops fitting. The consumer misses its deadline and leaves the group. The assignment is released through onPartitionsLost, so the in-flight batch was never committed and the next owner reprocesses it.

The consumer rejoins and asks for the same batch size without any changes to config. It misses the deadline again. This continues until the slowdown ends. A shared dependency degrades for all members at once, so they hit it together and the group rebalances repeatedly. The common response is a process restart after increasing max.poll.interval.ms or decreasing max.poll.records, which reassigns every group in that JVM.

The existing levers do not help. pause() postpones records without reducing them, so SmallRye's Kafka connector pauses partitions for backpressure and keeps its own queue, sized at max.poll.records times a factor. Spring Integration's KafkaMessageSource returns one record per receive(), so it rewrites the user's ConsumerFactory with max.poll.records=1 or refuses to start; allowMultiFetch instead buffers the batch and drains it one record at a time, and the documentation then warns you to process the batch and poll again within max.poll.interval.ms.

max.poll.interval.ms does two jobs. It detects a dead member, and it gives a live member headroom. It is also not local: the consumer sends it to the coordinator as a rebalance timeout, so it sets how long the rest of the group waits for this member to hand its partitions back, and varying it per call would change that wait for everyone else. It is unchanged by this proposal.

max.poll.records is read inside the consumer and sent nowhere, and it is already only a maximum, because the consumer returns fewer records whenever fewer are buffered. Choosing it on each call changes when the value is picked rather than what it means. An application measures its own throughput and knows whether a smaller batch means less work. This KIP lets it set the batch size per call.

Public Interfaces

javaPollOptions.java * Instances are mutable and may be reused. The consumer reads the values on entry and retains no * reference, so a caller may vary {@code maxRecords} between calls. The consumer is not thread-safe, * and neither is this class. */ @InterfaceAudience.Public public class PollOptions { /** The maximum time to block (must not be greater than {@link Long#MAX_VALUE} milliseconds) */ public static PollOptions timeout(Duration timeout) { ... } /** * Return at most this many records, from 0 up. Zero returns none. The consumer applies the lesser of * this and {@code max.poll.records}. Absent means {@code max.poll.records}. */ public PollOptions withMaxRecords(int maxRecords) { ... } /** The maximum time to block (must not be greater than {@link Long#MAX_VALUE} milliseconds) */ public Duration timeout() { ... } /** * Return at most this many records, from 0 up. Zero returns none. The consumer applies the lesser of * this and {@code max.poll.records}. Absent means {@code max.poll.records}. */ public OptionalInt maxRecords() { ... } }]]>

max.poll.records

No change to the default, the type or the behaviour. The documentation gains a sentence naming the per-call override:

javamax.poll.records

Consumer

javaConsumer.java poll(PollOptions options);]]>

KafkaConsumer

javaConsumer.java * At most {@link PollOptions#maxRecords()} records are returned. The effective limit is the lesser of that value and * {@code max.poll.records}, so a call may ask for fewer records than the configured value but not more; when * {@code maxRecords} is absent the configured value applies. The options object is not modified, so * {@link PollOptions#maxRecords()} still reports what the caller asked for, and one instance passed to two consumers * configured differently may resolve differently. *

* Records not returned stay buffered and are returned by a later call. They are not re-fetched and are not * deserialized. *

* Choosing the limit is the caller's decision. The signal is the time the previous batch took divided by the number * of records it returned. A caller whose cost is fixed per call rather than per record, such as a single flush or a * single insert, gains nothing from a smaller batch and should not reduce it. * * @param options the timeout for this call, and optionally the maximum number of records to return * * @return map of topic to records since the last fetch for the subscribed list of topics and partitions * * @throws java.lang.IllegalArgumentException if the timeout is negative, or {@code maxRecords} is negative * @throws ... and every other exception documented on {@link #poll(Duration)} */ @Override public ConsumerRecords poll(final PollOptions options);]]>

Metrics

Five metrics in the consumer-metrics group, tagged client-id. They are for an operator reading JMX. An application sizes the limit from its own clock.

MetricGroupTypeMeaning
poll-interval-remaining-msconsumer-metricsgaugeTime left before the poll interval expires.
poll-budget-used-ratio-avg, -maxconsumer-metricssampledProcessing time between polls, as a fraction of max.poll.interval.ms.
records-per-poll-avg, -maxconsumer-metricssampledRecords returned per call.
configured-max-poll-recordsconsumer-metricsgaugeThe configured max.poll.records. Constant.
effective-max-poll-recordsconsumer-metricsgaugeLimit in force on the last call.


  • A metric already in consumer-metrics look close, but does not answer the question, which is how much of the deadline is left right now.
  • last-poll-seconds-ago counts seconds since the last poll() invocation rather than since the poll timer reset, so it diverges from the deadline for a caller using a long timeout.
  • configured-max-poll-records never changes. It is there so the ceiling and the limit actually in force plot on one chart, which is what shows how far a member has backed off.

Proposed Changes

Same shape as CloseOptions in this package: private constructor, static factory, build pattern to mutate. It is mutable so a caller can hold one instance and change maxRecords between calls rather than rebuilding it. The timeout comes from the factory and is required. There is no default poll timeout to fall back on. maxRecords is OptionalInt; absent means max.poll.records. withMaxRecords stores the value without validating it, as CloseOptions.withTimeout does. Negative values are rejected by poll(). A call to poll() can take less work than the configured value, never more, so an application that adopts this cannot end up with larger batches than it has today. The bound is applied inside poll() rather than at the setter, because PollOptions is built without a consumer and cannot read max.poll.records.

FetchCollector takes the limit as a parameter in addition to the FetchBuffer, passed down from the poll() method for both Classic and Async KafkaConsumer. FetchConfig is unchanged.

poll(Duration) resolves the limit to max.poll.records and calls the same code, so there is one implementation rather than two.

Changing the limit between calls is safe, because stopping early leaves nothing half-done. The fetch position advances only for records actually returned. A fetch that was only partly drained stays where it is and is not initialised again. Records left behind are not deserialised.

An application has two places to act.

  • It sizes the next call from what the last one cost, using its own clock and the record count it received.
  • After an eviction, RebalanceCause.POLL_TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED from KIP-1364 identifies the cause in the rebalance callback, so the member comes back sized for the load that evicted it.

Zero is a legal limit. It returns no records and still resets the poll interval, which is the state a consumer already reaches when it has no data or all its partitions are paused. The bound does not interfere: the effective limit is the lesser of the per-call value and max.poll.records, and max.poll.records is never below 1, so a per-call zero always wins. Zero is legal per call but not as a config, because a permanent zero would leave a partition buffered forever and stop fetches to its leader, so max.poll.records keeps its existing lower bound of 1.

A zero limit gives a caller a way to stay in the group without taking work. poll(PollOptions.timeout(ZERO).withMaxRecords(0)) resets the poll interval and returns nothing, where poll(Duration.ZERO) can return a full batch the caller must then hold alongside the one it is processing. Today a framework reaches the same state with pause(assignment) and then poll(ZERO). A zero limit does not touch pause, so the application keeps it.

Edge Cases

Cases this change affects directly, and cases it does not fix.

  • A unit of work larger than the budget. No batch size fits one record whose processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms. Raising that value remains the remedy.
  • Slow rebalance callbacks. These run inside poll(), so a long onPartitionsAssigned consumes the poll interval where the caller cannot act.
  • Lag. A consumer that cannot keep up still falls behind however, the current metrics can highlight to operators why consumers fail to keep up with the batches.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

Consumer gains an abstract method, so every implementation must add it. Kafka has 5: KafkaConsumer, ClassicKafkaConsumer, AsyncKafkaConsumer,  MockConsumer, and Streams' abstract ConsumerWrapper. Callers are unaffected, and one that supplies no limit gets max.poll.records as before.

No configuration is added or deprecated, and no default changes. max.poll.records keeps its type, default and behaviour; only its documentation gains a sentence. There is no wire protocol change and no broker change.

The limit applies under both group protocols and to assign().

Test Plan

  • A supplied limit bounds the returned batch, is reduced to max.poll.records when larger than it, and rejects negative values.
  • effective-max-poll-records reports the lesser of the two after a call that asked for more than the configured value.
  • poll(Duration) and poll(PollOptions) return the same records for the same effective limit.
  • One reused PollOptions, mutated between calls, takes effect on each. The consumer retains no reference to it.
  • Changing the limit across two calls draining one buffered fetch produces no gap, duplicate or reorder. Same across a pause and resume.
  • A limit of zero returns no records, resets the poll interval, and leaves the buffered fetch intact for the next call. A member polling only with zero stays in the group past max.poll.interval.ms.
  • Each new gauge stays readable after a minute with no poll, and configured-max-poll-records reports the configured value. All new metrics are removed on close.

Rejected Alternatives

An adaptive policy inside the consumer, sizing the batch from observed processing time. A consumer cannot tell whether processing cost scales with the batch. When processing time is independent of batch size, reducing the size only deteriorates throughput. The application is better suited to tune the limit, by counting the time spent per batch.

Moving processing off the polling thread. This works, and SmallRye Reactive Messaging does it: a dedicated poll thread, a queue, and emission elsewhere, so the interval cannot expire from slow processing. It is the structurally correct fix, and KafkaConsumer's own javadoc recommends it. What it costs is a buffer with no bound the framework can enforce, and pause as the only brake on filling it.

A second poll parameter rather than an options object. KIP-41 considered a per-call limit and noted that overloading poll() "would arguably make the API more confusing". An options object adds one method, and needs no further overload when another per-call hint is proposed.

A per-call value that replaces max.poll.records rather than bounding it. Every other per-call override on this interface works that way. commitSync, committed, position, listTopics, partitionsFor, offsetsForTimes, beginningOffsets, endOffsets andclose Each take a default from configuration and use a caller's value as given, with default.api.timeout.ms supplying the default. A bound can be loosened later; it cannot be added later.

Buffering inside a ConsumerInterceptor. The technique works: cache every record, return an adaptive sublist from onConsume, release the rest on later calls. It is rejected on chaining, since an interceptor named in interceptor.classes would decide how much work the application receives. This involves interleaving multiple interceptors and synchronising between interceptors to ensure the buffering interceptor remains at the head, and even that cannot be guaranteed within frameworks, o11y javaagents that can inject their own via ByteBuddy instrumentation.

results.title: KIP-1387: Distribution Snapshots for Kafka client metrics

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under discussion

Discussion thread: here


JIRA: ASF JIRA5aa69414-a9e9-3523-82ec-879b028fb15bKAFKA-21361

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

Kafka clients report latency and size as an average and a maximum over a 30-second window, and nothing else reaches a MetricsReporter. clients/src/main/java uses new Avg() 36 times, new Max() 31 times, and Percentiles never, so no client latency or size metric has a percentile today.

An average and a maximum are useful, but they don't show how the values are spread out. Say a producer's requests mostly take 3 to 7 ms, and one request in the window stalls for 2 seconds. The average jumps to about 150 ms, which no longer looks like a normal request. Neither number tells you that most requests finished under 7 ms, or whether the stall was a one-off or the start of a problem. Fetch sizes have the same problem: they stay small while a consumer keeps up and jump when it reads a backlog, so the average lands between the two but does not represent either scenario (low steady state and peaks during lag).

You can't work out p50 or p99 from an average and a maximum. Kafka's Percentiles stat can compute them, but no client metric currently uses it. Using it would mean adding new metrics, which needs a KIP of its own, and it would still give only the few percentiles someone picked in advance, each over the same 30-second window: A p99 for the last 30 seconds can't be combined into a p99 for the hour.

This KIP adds one stat that counts how many values fell into each range, or bin, and gives those counts to the reporter. The reporter can then decide which percentiles to compute and over what period, or publish the raw bin counts to a downstream collector. A Prometheus reporter can publish the counts as _bucket, _sum and _count, an OpenTelemetry reporter can publish them as a histogram, and the client's own telemetry (KIP-714) could send a real histogram instead of single numbers.

Public Interfaces

javaDistributionSnapshot.javajavaDistributionStat.java { }]]>javaDistribution.javajavaGeometricBinScheme.javaThis is an upper-inclusive scheme by default, so it must not be used with {@link Percentiles} or * {@link Histogram}, whose arithmetic assumes lower-inclusive bins. */ @InterfaceAudience.Public public class GeometricBinScheme implements Histogram.BinScheme { private final int bins; private final double min; private final int scale; private final double[] edges; /** * @param bins total bins, including the zero, {@code (0, min]} and overflow bins; at least 4 * @param min the upper edge of bin 1; a power of two the scheme's own steps reach from 1.0 * @param scale the factor exponent, in {@code [-10, 20]} * @throws IllegalArgumentException if {@code min} falls between two steps, or the top finite edge overflows */ public GeometricBinScheme(int bins, double min, int scale) { ... } @Override public int bins() { return bins; } @Override public int toBin(double value) { ... } /** The lower edge of bin {@code bin}, so bin {@code b} is {@code (fromBin(b), fromBin(b + 1)]}. */ @Override public double fromBin(int bin) { ... } @Override public boolean upperInclusive() { return true; } }]]>

Bin 0 is only for zero, which is a common value for record-queue-time. That way a metric that only ever records zero reports zero, rather than a percentile somewhere between 0 and 1. Bin 1 holds everything above zero up to min.

Every client must compute the bin edges in exactly the same way, because a backend adds up buckets from different clients only when their edges match exactly.

Changes to existing types

The existing bin schemes, ConstantBinScheme and LinearBinScheme, include a bin's lower edge and exclude its upper edge, [low, high). The new scheme does the opposite, (low, high]. This definition aligns with many metric libraries such as  Prometheus and OpenTelemetry. So Histogram.BinScheme gets a method that says which kind a scheme is. It defaults to the existing kind (false), so current and third-party schemes keep working. Distribution refuses a scheme of lower-bounds, so a mistake fails when the metric is registered instead of quietly producing wrong buckets.

java

ConstantBinScheme and LinearBinScheme each get a constructor that takes upperInclusive. The existing constructors keep false, so nothing that uses them changes. ratio() uses an upper-inclusive constant bin scheme. ConstantBinScheme, because the precision that matters for a ratio is the same everywhere: 0.30 against 0.35 matters as much as 0.90 against 0.95


KafkaMetric gets a method that tells a reporter whether a metric is a distribution, without reading its value:

javaKafkaMetric.java

Sensor gets a method to register a distribution. It is a new method rather than another add, because it behaves differently: it registers nothing when the client's recording level is lower than the distribution's, for example a DEBUG distribution on a client running at INFO, and someone reading the code should be able to see that. It checks the distribution's own level, not the sensor's, because the sensors these distributions attach to are usually INFO even when a distribution should only exist at DEBUG.

javaSensor.java

A quota compares a metric's single value against a limit every time a value is recorded (Sensor.checkQuotas). A distribution has no single value, so checkQuotas skips it

metrics.distribution.scale

This KIP adds one client config, defined in CommonClientConfigs and available in ProducerConfig, ConsumerConfig and AdminClientConfig.



Typeint
Default2
Valid values[-1, 8]
Importancelow
DocBin resolution for distribution metrics. Bins grow by a factor of 2^(2^-scale), so a higher scale gives finer bins and more of them.

The number of bins is ceil(d * 2^scale) + 3, where d is how many times the range doubles. latencyMs() covers 1 ms to 65,536 ms, which is 16 doublings, and longLatencyMs() covers 1 ms to 1,048,576 ms, which is 20. The lowest allowed scale is -1, where each bin is four times as wide as the one before; anything coarser is too rough to use.

scale2^scaleeach bin isbins, latencyMs() (d = 16)bins, longLatencyMs() (d = 20)max quantile error
-10.54× the last16 × 0.5 + 3 = 1120 × 0.5 + 3 = 13300%
012× the last16 × 1 + 3 = 1920 × 1 + 3 = 23100%
241.19× the last16 × 4 + 3 = 6720 × 4 + 3 = 8319%
4161.04× the last16 × 16 + 3 = 25920 × 16 + 3 = 3234%

The config only changes latency distributions. Size distributions always use scale 0, where each bin is twice the last, because byte sizes are usually powers of two and scale 0 puts them exactly on bin edges. Ratio distributions use bins of equal width, so the scale doesn't apply to them.

Most fleets should keep the default, 2, where each bin is about 19% wider than the one before. Raise it to 4 to tell apart latencies that differ by less than that, at about four times as many series. Lower it to 0 for fewer series, if bins that double are precise enough. Whoever runs the metrics backend for a fleet makes this choice, once, for every client that reports to it.

It has to be one value for the whole fleet. When a query combines histograms from many clients, it adds up buckets that have the same bounds. Clients on different scales have different bounds, so the combined histogram is wrong, and nothing warns you: the query still returns a number. While a scale change rolls out, fleet-wide percentiles are wrong until every client has the new value. Queries about a single client are not affected.

Proposed Changes

Counts are cumulative, not windowed

Every other client stat covers a recent window of time. A distribution doesn't: it counts from the moment it is created.

That is because Prometheus and OpenTelemetry understand only two kinds of counts: a running total, or the change since the last read. A sliding window is neither. When old values drop out of the window the total goes down, and both formats take that to mean the client restarted.

A reporter that wants a window can subtract an earlier snapshot from a later one with minus(). If startTimeMs() is later than it was at the previous read, the distribution was recreated and its counts started again from zero.

Why geometric bins

Kafka already counts values in bins: Percentiles and Frequencies both do. This KIP adds one more way of laying out bins, and gives the bin counts to the reporter instead of turning them into a few numbers.

Each bin is a fixed percentage wider than the one before, because latencies and sizes range from tiny to huge. With bins of equal width you would need a huge number of them to see small values clearly, or you would lose all detail at the small end. Bins that grow keep the same relative precision everywhere with a modest number of bins.

The growth is set by a whole-number scale, the same way OpenTelemetry's exponential histograms set theirs. A bin includes its upper edge, because that is what a bucket bound means in both Prometheus and OpenTelemetry.

Where to use it

Each distribution sits next to the existing -avg and -max metrics and replaces nothing. There is one per client, tagged only with client-id, and named like its -avg and -max but with a -distribution suffix.

Seven distributions are on by default, at INFO, The DEBUG ones are likely to be useful during investigation. They are here so that an operator can turn them on with metrics.recording.level=DEBUG without waiting for another KIP, and they are disabled otherwise.

GroupMetricSchemeLevelBins
producer-metricsrequest-latencylatencyMs()INFO67
producer-metricsrecord-queue-timelongLatencyMs()INFO83
producer-metricsbatch-sizesizeBytes()INFO33
producer-metricsrecord-sizesizeBytes()INFO33
producer-metricscompression-ratioratio()INFO22
consumer-fetch-manager-metricsfetch-latencylatencyMs()INFO67
consumer-fetch-manager-metricsfetch-sizesizeBytes()INFO33
producer-metricsproduce-throttle-timelatencyMs()DEBUG67
consumer-fetch-manager-metricsfetch-throttle-timelatencyMs()DEBUG67
consumer-coordinator-metricscommit-latencylatencyMs()DEBUG67
consumer-coordinator-metricsrebalance-latencylongLatencyMs()DEBUG83
consumer-coordinator-metricsjoin-timelongLatencyMs()DEBUG83
consumer-coordinator-metricssync-timelongLatencyMs()DEBUG83
consumer-coordinator-metricspartition-{revoked,assigned,lost}-latencylatencyMs()DEBUG3 × 67
consumer-metricstime-between-polllongLatencyMs()DEBUG83
consumer-metricspoll-idle-ratioratio()DEBUG22


Each distribution is one more metric per client. At the default level that is five more for a producer and two for a consumer, and at DEBUG six and twelve. How a reporter ships a distribution's bin edges and counts is up to the reporter.

Each distribution records exactly what its existing sensor records with a few caveats:

  • request-latency is measured in whole milliseconds, so a request that takes under 1 ms, which is common inside one datacenter and rack-aware pipelines. It is recorded as 0 and counted in the zero bin. For this metric, the distribution is most useful for the slow requests.
  • record-queue-time and record-size are recorded each time a batch is sent, so the records in a retried batch are counted again.
  • commit-latency also records commits that fail.
  • compression-ratio is recorded by the sensor behind compression-rate-avg, which is a ratio despite its name, so the distribution uses the accurate name. It is a batch's compressed size divided by its uncompressed size, recorded once per batch, so a value above 1 means the batch grew. One client's distribution covers all the topic-partitions it writes to.
  • poll-idle-ratio is recorded once per poll: the share of time the consumer spent inside poll() rather than waiting for the application to process the last records. A value near 0 means the application is the bottleneck.
  • fetch-latency includes fetches that wait the full fetch.max.wait.ms, 500 ms by default, because there is nothing to read. An idle consumer therefore shows a cluster of values around 500 ms, apart from the fetches that return data.
  • record-queue-time, time-between-poll and the rebalance timers (rebalance-latency, join-time, sync-time) can run past a minute, up to delivery.timeout.ms (2 minutes by default) or max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes by default), so they use longLatencyMs() i.e. so up to 17min of resolution.

Today Kafka registers every metric whatever the recording level, and only skips recording into it. That is fine for a single number, but an unused DEBUG distribution would still export dozens of empty series. So addDistribution doesn't register a distribution at all below its level. Existing metrics don't change.

Distributions go only on per-client metrics, not per-connection ones. Per-connection metrics (Selector.maybeRegisterConnectionMetrics) are removed only when the client closes, so per-connection distributions would keep piling up as connections come and go. That is why the per-node request-latency and request-size don't map to a distribution stat.

Out of Scope

This KIP adds distributions only to producer and consumer metrics. Brokers, including the group coordinator, could use the same stat, and so could frameworks built on the clients, such as Connect and Streams. Each of those has its own metrics and owners, so they are left to follow-up KIPs. They can use Distribution as it is.

Exporting

The bins map directly onto the histogram formats of Prometheus and OpenTelemetry. Kafka's bin i is OpenTelemetry's bucket i, since both include their upper edge. Prometheus labels each bucket with its upper edge, le, so bin i gets le = binEdge(i + 1), and the last one is +Inf. A reporter needs the edges as well as the counts, which is why the snapshot includes them.

The snapshot doesn't support OpenTelemetry's exponential histogram format, which is why it publishes edges rather than the scale. Bin 1 covers everything between zero and min, and the last bin has no upper edge; the exponential format can't represent either.

Sending distributions through Kafka's own client telemetry (KIP-714) is left for a follow-up change. It needs no KIP, because it only touches internal classes: one branch in KafkaMetricsCollector and a histogram(...) builder in SinglePointMetric. Until then the telemetry collector skips distributions, as it already skips any metric that isn't a single number.

Temporality

Reporters should export the counts as running totals (cumulative), which is how they are kept.

Exporting only the change since the last read (deltas) can lose data. A metric can go quiet for minutes, as record-queue-time does when a producer is idle. A backend that adds deltas back up into totals, as Prometheus does, may treat the first value after a quiet gap as the start of a new series, and rate() and increase() ignore the first point of a series, so that value is lost. A reporter that has to send deltas can avoid this by sending one, from minus(), at every collection, even when it is zero.

Either way, if startTimeMs() is later than at the previous read, the counts have restarted.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

  • Existing stats, such as Histogram, Percentiles and SampledStat, don't change. Histogram.BinScheme.upperInclusive() defaults to false, so existing and third-party schemes keep working. TThe other changes are additions: KafkaMetric.isDistribution(), Sensor.addDistribution, constructors on ConstantBinScheme and LinearBinScheme, and the quota check skipping distributions.

  • isMeasurable() still means that metricValue() returns a Double because a class can't be both a DistributionStat and a MeasurableStat. A reporter that wants distributions checks for a DistributionSnapshot value, or calls isDistribution(). Reporters already have to cope with values that aren't numbers, such as app-info's version, which is a string.

  • JmxReporter skips distributions, because JMX expects every Kafka metric attribute to be a double. It logs this once at debug level.

  • One javadoc fix: BinScheme.fromBin returns a bin's lower edge, but its javadoc says upper.

Test Plan

  • GeometricBinScheme gives exactly the same edges on every JVM. Zero goes in bin 0, the smallest value above zero in bin 1, and a value exactly on an edge in the bin that ends at that edge.
  • Values beyond either end go in the first or last bin, and the constructor rejects arguments it can't support.
  • An upper-inclusive ConstantBinScheme puts a ratio exactly on an edge, such as 0.05 or 1.0, in the bin that ends there, and a ratio above 1 in the last bin. The existing constructors of both schemes behave as before.
  • Distribution records ordinary values and ignores NaN, infinite and negative ones.
  • Counts stay correct for a long-lived distribution.
  • quantile() never returns less than the true value. It returns NaN when the distribution is empty and infinity when the answer is in the last bin.
  • minus() returns the counts recorded between two reads, and null if the distribution was recreated or its bins changed in between.
  • Registering a distribution on a real Metrics instance doesn't break the existing reporters.
  • A distribution above the client's recording level isn't registered, even when its sensor is INFO, and a distribution on a sensor with a quota doesn't throw.
  • A histogram built from a snapshot matches the one Prometheus or OpenTelemetry builds from the same values.

Rejected Alternatives

Windowed snapshots, by extending SampledStat, as a first draft did. Neither Prometheus nor OpenTelemetry can represent a sliding window.

A delta stat that resets when it is read. A client can have several reporters, and nothing coordinates their reads, so each read would take counts away from the other reporters.

Exponential histograms, which OpenTelemetry and Prometheus native histograms use. These have resizable bins but it makes the series export on the Kafka client hard to reason with. Fixed bins keep three things simple instead: each distribution uses the same memory whatever it records, every client has the same bin bounds, so any backend can add them up. This KIP is already a large change, and fixed bins keep the rest of it simple.

Putting the bin scheme or scale on the snapshot. It would only help the exponential format, rejected above.

Overloading Sensor.add instead of adding addDistribution. sensor.add(name, null) would match both methods and stop compiling, and it would be easy to miss that the new method behaves differently below the recording level.

Exposing the bins over JMX as a structured value (CompositeData), so tools like jconsole could read them. Left out to keep this KIP small; it can be added later without changing this API.

Adding a method to Percentiles. Percentiles registers one metric per percentile, so having it return a whole distribution would mix two different things in one class.

Changing Histogram, Percentiles or Frequencies. Histogram.counts() is public and returns float[], so moving to the long counts a running total needs would break it. Percentiles and Frequencies are CompoundStats, which can only expose single numbers, not bins, and making them cumulative would change the metrics their users already have. Keeping their samples instead of dropping them would grow memory without limit. New classes change nothing that exists.

More percentiles registered. Someone would still have to choose them in advance.

HdrHistogram. More accurate, but every producer and consumer would get a new dependency.

results.title: KIP-1388: Add a committed-offsets filter to ListGroups

storage.value:
Status

Current state: Under Discussion

Discussion thread: here

JIRA: KAFKA-21366

Please keep the discussion on the mailing list rather than commenting on the wiki (wiki discussions get unwieldy fast).

Motivation

Tools that replicate consumer group offsets between clusters typically use two RPCs, with client-side filtering in between:

  1. Admin.listGroups(ListGroupsOptions.forConsumerGroups()) (the ListGroups RPC, sent to every broker) to enumerate the consumer groups on the source cluster.
  2. Apply a user-supplied group filter (an allow list, deny list or pattern) to the listed group ids.
  3. Admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets(...) (the OffsetFetch RPC, batched per group coordinator) for the groups that passed the filter.

MirrorMaker 2 does exactly this in MirrorCheckpointConnector, and the group offset synchronization in KIP-1279 (Cluster Mirroring) follows the same pattern. Other cross-cluster replication tools built on the Admin API do the same.

A group exists in the group coordinator while it has at least one member or at least one committed offset; a group with neither is removed by the periodic group cleanup. In some scenarios, a large number of the groups returned by ListGroups have members but no committed offsets at all. Typical examples are:

  • consumers that disable auto-commit and never commit, for example because they store offsets outside Kafka, or because they are short-lived command-line consumers such as kafka-console-consumer.sh;
  • consumers that have joined a group but have not committed yet, which is a permanent condition for applications that only read and never commit.

In some large deployments, we have seen thousands of such groups. For each of them, the replication tool still fetches offsets, receives nothing and discards the group. OffsetFetch can carry several groups per request to a coordinator, but every offset-less group still costs coordinator work, response bytes and client-side handling.

ListGroups already supports server-side filtering by group state (KIP-518) and by group type (KIP-848). The group coordinator holds both the group metadata and the committed offsets of a group in the same coordinator shard, so it can answer "does this group have any committed offsets?" with a local lookup while it builds the ListGroups response. This KIP adds that filter.

The change is deliberately made to the newer Admin.listGroups API introduced by KIP-1043 and not to Admin.listConsumerGroups, which has been deprecated since 4.1.

Public Interfaces

Client API changes

ListGroupsOptions

A new filter is added to org.apache.kafka.clients.admin.ListGroupsOptions.

java { /** * If set to true, only groups that have at least one committed offset will be returned by listGroups(). * Otherwise, groups are returned whether or not they have committed offsets. * This operation is supported by brokers with version 4.5.0 or later. */ public ListGroupsOptions requireCommittedOffsets(boolean requireCommittedOffsets); /** * Returns true if only groups with committed offsets are requested. */ public boolean requireCommittedOffsets(); } ]]>

The default value is false , which preserves the existing behavior.

Example: list all consumer groups that have committed offsets.

java groups = admin.listGroups( ListGroupsOptions.forConsumerGroups().requireCommittedOffsets(true) ).all().get();]]>

all() is used so that a broker that does not support the filter fails the call instead of silently returning a partial listing (see the compatibility section).

No changes are made to Admin, ListGroupsResult or GroupListing.

Kafka protocol changes

ListGroups API

The ListGroups API is bumped to version 6. The request gains one field. The response is unchanged, and its version is bumped only to keep request and response versions aligned.

Request schema
json
Response schema
json

No new error codes are introduced.

Proposed Changes

Group coordinator

When a ListGroups request has RequireCommittedOffsets set to true, the group coordinator returns only groups with at least one committed offset. This condition is combined with the existing state and type filters using AND semantics.

A group matches if the committed state of its group coordinator contains a committed offset for at least one topic partition of that group. The offset predicate and the existing state filter are evaluated consistently against the coordinator’s committed state.

Pending transactional offsets do not count because the transaction may still abort. A group with only pending offsets becomes eligible once the transaction commits and the resulting offsets take effect in the coordinator’s committed state. A group with an existing committed offset continues to match even if it also has pending transactional offsets.

Group’s offset stateMatches
At least one committed offset, whether or not pending transactional offsets also existYes
Only pending transactional offsetsNo
Neither committed nor pending offsetsNo

Offsets eligible for expiration continue to count until their deletion takes effect in the coordinator’s committed state. Once deletion of the last committed offset takes effect, the group no longer matches.

The predicate concerns stored committed offsets, not the offsets visible to a particular caller through OffsetFetch, which also applies authorization and stability checks.

The coordinator creates group metadata when processing an offset commit for an unknown group ID, so offset-only groups are included in the group metadata that ListGroups enumerates. The new filter adds a per-group in-memory existence check; it does not enumerate the group’s topic partitions or require additional external I/O.

The filter considers only offsets stored by the group coordinator. It is applicable to Classic, Consumer, and Streams groups. Share-group consumption state is maintained separately by the share coordinator and does not count toward this predicate. Share groups therefore do not match, and ListGroupsOptions.forShareGroups().requireCommittedOffsets(true) returns an empty result. Querying share-group consumption state is outside the scope of this KIP.

Admin client

ListGroupsOptions gets a new option. When it is set, the admin client sets the new field in the ListGroups request. The request is sent with version 6 or later. If a broker does not support version 6, the request to that broker fails with UnsupportedVersionException, because the client cannot emulate the filter without fetching the offsets of every group, which is exactly the cost this KIP removes. The field is deliberately not ignorable; see Rejected Alternatives. listGroups is asynchronous and fans out to every broker, so this failure surfaces through ListGroupsResult: all() completes exceptionally with the first failure, errors() contains one Throwable per failed broker, and valid() contains the groups from the brokers that succeeded. When the option is not set, the request is unchanged and continues to work with brokers of any version supported by the client.

The authorization model of ListGroups is unchanged: a principal with DESCRIBE on the cluster receives all groups, otherwise only groups the principal has DESCRIBE on. The new filter only removes groups from that set. Note that this exposes one additional bit of information per listed group, namely whether the group has committed offsets, to any principal that can list the group. A principal with cluster DESCRIBE but without DESCRIBE on a given group can learn this bit although OffsetFetch for that group would be denied. The filter does not reveal which topics have offsets or the offset values themselves, which continue to require DESCRIBE on the group and on the topics. We consider this acceptable because the existence of committed offsets is comparable to the group state and group type that ListGroups already returns, but we call it out explicitly for review.

Command-line tools

No command-line tool changes are proposed. kafka-groups.sh --list and kafka-consumer-groups.sh --list continue to list all groups.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

  • Existing clients against new brokers: unaffected. Clients that send ListGroups version 5 or earlier do not set the new field, and the broker treats the filter as disabled.
  • New clients against existing brokers: unaffected unless the new option is used. ListGroupsOptions.requireCommittedOffsets(true) requires ListGroups version 6. Against a broker that does not support version 6 the request to that broker fails with UnsupportedVersionException, consistent with how the states filter from KIP-518 behaves against brokers that predate it. Because listGroups is asynchronous, the exception is not thrown by the method call; it is the cause of the ExecutionException from all().get(), and it appears in errors(). Callers that must support older brokers should check that the cause is UnsupportedVersionException (the same exception can also come from another unsupported filter, so the retry can fail again and that failure must propagate) and then retry the listing without requireCommittedOffsets, keeping their state, type and protocol-type filters. Callers that use valid() must also inspect errors(), otherwise an unsupported broker looks like a broker with no groups.
  • Behavior of existing calls: the default value of the option is false, so the set of groups returned by Admin.listGroups and the command-line tools does not change.
  • Deprecation: nothing is deprecated. The option is intentionally not added to the deprecated Admin.listConsumerGroups API or ListConsumerGroupsOptions.
  • Mixed-version clusters: Admin.listGroups sends one ListGroups request to every broker and negotiates the version per broker. During a rolling upgrade some brokers support version 6 and some do not. The requests to the older brokers fail with UnsupportedVersionException; all() fails, errors() reports one failure per such broker, and valid() contains only the groups from the upgraded brokers. A tool that needs a complete listing must therefore either fail closed on all() or, for that round, retry with only the committed-offset filter disabled and every other option unchanged, as described above. It must not treat valid() alone as complete.

Test Plan

  • Unit tests for the group coordinator (GroupMetadataManager / GroupCoordinatorShard) that verify the filter in combination with the states and types filters, for groups with committed offsets, groups with no offsets, groups with only pending transactional offsets, groups with both committed and pending transactional offsets, and groups whose offsets have expired but have not been cleaned up yet. Verify that a pending-only group becomes eligible after its transaction commits and the offsets take effect in committed state, and remains ineligible after abort if it has no other committed offsets.

  • Unit tests for ListGroupsRequest that verify the new field is rejected when the negotiated version is below 6 and the option is set, including when the types filter names only classic and consumer groups and would otherwise be downgraded, so that the new check is not bypassed by that early return; and that the request is unchanged when the option is not set.

  • KafkaAdminClient unit tests for listGroups with the new option, including the UnsupportedVersionException path.

  • Integration tests in the admin client integration test suite that create a consumer group with committed offsets and a consumer group with active members that never commit, and verify that only the former is returned when the option is set and both are returned otherwise.

  • Coordinator tests that verify the filter is evaluated against committed state: an offset insertion or deletion that has not yet taken effect in that state does not change the listing result.

  • Coordinator tests that a share group is never returned when the filter is set, and that a streams group with committed offsets is returned.

  • Authorization integration tests: a principal with cluster DESCRIBE only, and a principal with DESCRIBE on some groups only, receive the filtered subset of the groups they are allowed to list.

  • Mixed-version tests: with the filter set, all() fails and errors() reports the brokers that do not support version 6, while valid() contains the groups from the brokers that do.

  • Protocol compatibility tests for the new ListGroups version.

Rejected Alternatives

Extend Admin.listConsumerGroupOffsets / OffsetFetch to return the offsets of all groups

This would replace the two-step pattern with a single call. It is a much larger change: OffsetFetch is addressed to a specific group coordinator and routed by group id, so an "all groups" variant would need a new routing model, pagination for potentially very large responses, and a way to express the group filter that replication tools apply between the two steps. The two-step approach also lets the tool filter groups before any offsets are fetched. Filtering out offset-less groups in ListGroups solves the practical problem with a one-field change.

Add the filter to the deprecated Admin.listConsumerGroups API

listConsumerGroups and ListConsumerGroupsOptions have been deprecated since 4.1 in favor of listGroups (KIP-1043). New functionality should only be added to the replacement API.

Return a hasCommittedOffsets flag per group in the ListGroups response instead of a request filter

A response flag would let clients filter locally and would also be useful for tooling that displays groups. However, it does not reduce the size of the response for the replication use case, and the filtering use case is the one with the demonstrated cost. A response field can be added by a later KIP if a use case for it appears; the request filter proposed here does not prevent that.

Use the existing states filter

Group state does not indicate whether a group has committed offsets. Groups with active members may or may not have committed offsets, and those groups are exactly the ones replication tools must inspect. Groups in the Empty state usually have committed offsets, because the periodic group cleanup removes groups that have neither members nor offsets, but there is a window of up to offsets.retention.check.interval.ms where an Empty group has no offsets.

Make the filter a tri-state (all groups / only with offsets / only without offsets)

There is no known use case for listing only groups without committed offsets. A boolean keeps the API small. If such a use case appears, a new field can be added in a later version.

Add --with-committed-offsets to kafka-groups.sh --list

The motivating use case is programmatic. Keeping the tools unchanged keeps this KIP small. A tool flag can be added later without a protocol change.

Make the new request field ignorable

If RequireCommittedOffsets were marked "ignorable": true, the admin client would send version 5 to an older broker and that broker would return every group, so no caller-side handling would be needed. This was considered and rejected for two reasons. First, the admin client fails strictly whenever an option cannot be expressed in the negotiated protocol version, for example the states filter on ListGroups, requireStable on OffsetFetch and includeAuthorizedOperations on Metadata, and this filter should behave the same way. Second, the response has no way to indicate that the filter was not applied, so a caller could neither detect nor log that it was not getting the benefit; the exception is the only signal it has. The only silent downgrade in ListGroupsRequest today, for a types filter that names only classic and consumer groups, is lossless because older brokers have no other group types. Dropping this filter would not be lossless.

results.title: KIP-1389: Surface effective group configurations to clients

storage.value:
Status

  • Current state: Under Discussion
  • Discussion thread: https://lists.apache.org/thread/gctkxrg2y664jt4sq18znrgl0omd93tp
  • JIRA: KAFKA-20848
  • Release: TBD

Motivation

With the consumer group protocol (KIP-848), share groups (KIP-932) and the Streams rebalance protocol (KIP-1071), settings that shape how a client behaves are group configurations owned by the broker. Some of them, such as the session timeout and the heartbeat interval of consumer groups, used to be client configurations; others, such as a share group's record lock duration, were introduced as group configurations. Settings such as session timeouts and heartbeat intervals have broker-level defaults and bounds, and an administrator can override them for a single group. None of these values are set in the client's configuration.

The client sees only some of these values. The heartbeat responses of all three protocols carry the heartbeat interval, and the Streams heartbeat response also carries the task offset interval and the acceptable recovery lag. Clients recently started logging these values (KAFKA-20761 for consumer and share groups, and the equivalent change for Streams). A share consumer also receives the record lock duration in the ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge responses, as AcquisitionLockTimeoutMs, and exposes it through ShareConsumer#acquisitionLockTimeoutMs(). Other values, including the session timeout of every group type, are not included in any response. When diagnosing unexpected group behavior from the client's logs, one cannot tell which of these values the brokers are applying.

The values in effect can also differ from the configured ones. KIP-1240 lets a broker start even if a stored group configuration lies outside the broker's current bounds, and clamps the effective value to those bounds. The broker logs a warning when it does so, but the client is not told. In a reproduction attached to KAFKA-20848, consumer.session.timeout.ms was set to 60000 for a group, and the broker was then restarted with the session timeout bounds narrowed to 20000–30000 (group.consumer.min.session.timeout.ms=20000, group.consumer.session.timeout.ms=25000, group.consumer.max.session.timeout.ms=30000):

  • The broker logged that the value is capped to 30000.
  • Describing the group configuration still returned 60000, the stored value.
  • The consumer received no indication that its effective session timeout had been reduced, because the session timeout is not part of the heartbeat response.
  • After the consumer was killed, the member was fenced approximately 30 seconds after the coordinator processed its last heartbeat, so 30000 was the value in effect.

A user who chose 60 seconds to tolerate long pauses therefore sees members fenced after 30 seconds, and nothing on the client side explains why. Similar discrepancies between configured and effective values can arise when other settings are clamped to their lower or upper bounds, or when a group names a Streams task assignor that is not available and the coordinator falls back to the default assignor. Even for values that are sent to the client, such as the heartbeat interval or the record lock duration, the client receives the effective value but cannot tell that it differs from the configured one.

The protocols already carry this kind of information in places. The share fetch path sends the effective record lock duration to the client, and Streams uses the heartbeat response to report a misconfiguration: the MISSING_CLIENT_TAGS status (KAFKA-20744) tells a member that client tags required for rack-aware standby task assignment are missing. This KIP exposes the effective group configurations relevant to each protocol through responses from the broker that applies them. For the group heartbeats that broker is the group coordinator. The share configurations that govern record delivery, such as the record lock duration and the delivery count limit, are applied by each share partition leader against its own bounds and defaults, so they are reported in the ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge responses of the leader rather than in the share group heartbeat. Clients log these values on first receipt and when they change, and warn when a stored group override differs from the value in effect.

Public Interfaces

This KIP adds a new version of five RPCs. In each, the response gains two tagged fields, an opaque state token and a list of effective group configurations, and the request gains one tagged field to echo the token.

RPCCurrent versionsNew versionBroker that sends the listEntries
ConsumerGroupHeartbeat0-1N (2 today)group coordinator4
ShareGroupHeartbeat1N (2 today)group coordinator4
StreamsGroupHeartbeat0-1N (2 today)group coordinator11
ShareFetch1-2N (3 today)share partition leader8
ShareAcknowledge1-2N (3 today)share partition leader8

N is the next unreleased version of each RPC when this KIP is implemented. KIP-1313 introduces a new version of every RPC in Apache Kafka 4.5; if this KIP lands in the same release, the fields are added to that version in coordination with KAFKA-20925 instead of a separate bump (see Compatibility). The new fields are tagged because they are optional: the token is absent from responses with a top-level error, and after the first exchange the list is absent from most responses.

Request schema

The same field is added to ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest, ShareGroupHeartbeatRequest, StreamsGroupHeartbeatRequest, ShareFetchRequest and ShareAcknowledgeRequest. Shown for ConsumerGroupHeartbeatRequest:

// Version N adds GroupConfigsToken (KIP-1389).
{ "name": "GroupConfigsToken", "type": "int64", "versions": "N+", "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 0,
  "default": "-1", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The token of the group configurations the client holds for this broker, or -1 if it holds none." }

Response schema

The same fields are added to ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse, ShareGroupHeartbeatResponse, StreamsGroupHeartbeatResponse, ShareFetchResponse and ShareAcknowledgeResponse. Shown for ConsumerGroupHeartbeatResponse:

// Version N adds GroupConfigsToken and GroupConfigs (KIP-1389).
{ "name": "GroupConfigsToken", "type": "int64", "versions": "N+", "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 0,
  "default": "-1", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "Identifies the group configuration state of this broker for the group, or -1 if this response carries no group configuration information." },
{ "name": "GroupConfigs", "type": "[]EffectiveGroupConfig", "versions": "N+", "nullableVersions": "N+",
  "taggedVersions": "N+", "tag": 1, "default": "null", "ignorable": true,
  "about": "The effective group configurations applied by this broker, or null if they are unchanged from the state identified by the request's GroupConfigsToken.",
  "fields": [
    { "name": "Name", "type": "string", "versions": "N+",
      "about": "The group configuration name." },
    { "name": "Value", "type": "string", "versions": "N+",
      "about": "The effective value." },
    { "name": "ConfiguredValue", "type": "string", "versions": "N+", "nullableVersions": "N+", "default": "null",
      "about": "The value of the stored group override if it is not the value in effect, null otherwise." }
  ]
}

Tag numbers 0 and 1 are free in all ten schemas today; they are coordinated with any other KIP adding tagged fields to the same versions.

Field semantics

GroupConfigsToken (response)

  • -1: this response carries no group configuration information. A broker returns -1, with a null list, in any response with a top-level error (for example NOT_COORDINATOR or an authorization error), in any response where it cannot resolve the group, and in responses to a member leaving the group. Such a response does not change the client's cache.
  • Any other value: identifies the state of the exposed content (every entry's Name, Value and ConfiguredValue) on this broker. The value is opaque; clients store and echo it and never compute it. A broker never issues -1. Different states may in rare cases share a token (see Rejected Alternatives).

GroupConfigs (response)

  • Present: the full list for the token in the same response. Never empty.
  • Null with a token other than -1: the broker's current state is the one identified by the token in the request.
  • In a response that carries a token, a broker includes the list when the request's token is -1 or differs from its current token.

GroupConfigsToken (request)

  • The token the client holds, together with the list it identifies, for the broker it sends the request to; -1 if it holds none.

Entries

  • One entry per group configuration in the table below, for the RPC that carries it. A configuration added to Apache Kafka later is not included automatically.
  • Value is the configuration as resolved by the responding broker when it built the response, through the same resolution the broker uses for its behavior (overrides, broker defaults, bounds, fallbacks). It describes the configuration, not work already in progress: for example, a new record lock duration applies to locks acquired or renewed afterwards. For the dead letter queue configurations it is the configuration value, not a statement that the feature is enabled or used.
  • ConfiguredValue is non-null when a stored group override exists and is not the value in effect: because it was clamped to a broker bound (KIP-1240), or because streams.assignor.name names an assignor that is not available and the default assignor is used. Null does not mean that the group has no override, nor that no clamping happened anywhere: ConfiguredValue only reports stored group overrides, so when a dynamically updated broker default is clamped to the broker's own bounds, Value carries the clamped value and ConfiguredValue stays null.
  • Values are rendered from the parsed value: integers in plain decimal; booleans as true or false; strings in the documented configuration syntax; lists as the elements joined with commas in configured order; an empty string or list as the empty string.
  • Where a value is also sent in an existing field (HeartbeatIntervalMs, TaskOffsetIntervalMs, AcceptableRecoveryLag, AcquisitionLockTimeoutMs), both come from the same state and are equal. Clients keep using the existing fields for their behavior.
RPCGroup configurations
ConsumerGroupHeartbeatconsumer.session.timeout.ms, consumer.heartbeat.interval.ms, consumer.assignment.interval.ms, consumer.assignor.offload.enable
ShareGroupHeartbeatshare.session.timeout.ms, share.heartbeat.interval.ms, share.assignment.interval.ms, share.assignor.offload.enable
StreamsGroupHeartbeatstreams.session.timeout.ms, streams.heartbeat.interval.ms, streams.assignment.interval.ms, streams.assignor.offload.enable, streams.task.offset.interval.ms, streams.acceptable.recovery.lag, streams.num.standby.replicas, streams.num.warmup.replicas, streams.initial.rebalance.delay.ms, streams.rack.aware.assignment.tags, streams.assignor.name
ShareFetch, ShareAcknowledgeshare.record.lock.duration.ms, share.delivery.count.limit, share.partition.max.record.locks, share.renew.acknowledge.enable, share.auto.offset.reset, share.isolation.level, errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name, errors.deadletterqueue.copy.record.enable

Authorization

Existing RPC authorization is unchanged; no additional DESCRIBE_CONFIGS permission is required. Responses with a top-level error, including GROUP_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, carry no group configuration information. For ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge, partition-level errors, including TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, do not by themselves suppress the group configuration information. Authorized clients receive the effective values listed in this KIP and, where a stored override differs, that override's parsed value. The share list includes errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name, a topic name. Exposing this fixed set of configurations to the clients that the group serves is the intent of this proposal; describing group configurations keeps requiring DESCRIBE_CONFIGS.

Client logging

Log output is not a public API, but it is what users see, so the intended behavior is described here.

The protocol cache and the deduplication of log messages have the same scope and the same lifetime, per key:

PathScope and lifetime of the cache and the deduplication state
ConsumerGroupHeartbeat, ShareGroupHeartbeat, StreamsGroupHeartbeatOne key per group within a client instance. Cleared when the client explicitly leaves the group or closes.
ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledgeOne key per broker, shared by both RPCs. Kept as long as the client keeps local share session state for that broker, and discarded together with it.

Deduplication compares list contents and mismatches, not tokens: a list received with a new token but unchanged content is not logged again.

  • INFO when the list content held for a key changes, including the first list received for the key, with the group ID, the broker ID that reported it and every entry.
  • WARN when a mismatch, identified by (Name, ConfiguredValue, Value), is present in the list received for a key and was not present in the list previously held for that key. A different effective value for the same configuration is a different mismatch and is warned about separately. A mismatch is resolved for a key when the list held for that key no longer contains it; if it reappears later, it is warned about again. The message states the configured and the effective value without naming a cause, for example: Group configuration consumer.session.timeout.ms for group g1 has configured value 60000 but effective value 30000 on broker 1.
  • On the share path the same mismatch is therefore warned about once per broker whose leaders report it, and again after the client has discarded its local share session state for that broker and later establishes a new one. The lifetime of the deduplication state equals the lifetime of that local state; the misconfiguration itself may outlive it on the broker.

No client configurations, public Java APIs or metrics are added.

Proposed Changes

Broker

Keeping the configured values. Today the group configuration manager stores only the evaluated configuration of each group, after the stored overrides have been clamped to the broker bounds (KIP-1240). The broker also keeps the stored overrides, so that it can tell when an override is not the value in effect. Describing group configurations is not changed by this KIP.

Resolving the effective values. For every configuration in the table under Public Interfaces, the effective value is resolved through the same code path the broker uses for its behavior: the group override if present, otherwise the broker's own default, after clamping, and after fallbacks such as the default Streams task assignor when the configured one is not available. The diagnostic path does not reimplement any of these rules, and it does not emit the warnings that the regular path logs (for example, the warning for an unavailable task assignor).

Snapshots and tokens. For each group and each response type, the broker builds an immutable snapshot of the entries it reports: Name, Value and ConfiguredValue, rendered as described under Public Interfaces. All entries of one response, the token, and any existing field that carries the same value (such as HeartbeatIntervalMs or AcquisitionLockTimeoutMs) come from the same snapshot. The token is a 64-bit hash of the snapshot's content with entries sorted by name and a canonical encoding that keeps entry and string boundaries unambiguous. A token of -1 is never issued. Brokers using the same hash algorithm and canonical encoding produce the same token for identical snapshot contents, so a client that moves to another coordinator with the same content keeps its list without receiving it again. Different contents may produce the same token due to a hash collision (see Rejected Alternatives). The hash algorithm is an implementation detail; clients only echo the value.

A snapshot changes only when its exposed content changes. The inputs that can change it while the broker runs are the group's overrides and the dynamically reconfigurable broker defaults (the assignment interval and assignor offload configurations). Bounds, other broker defaults and the set of available task assignors only change across a restart. The snapshot can be cached per group and rebuilt when one of these inputs changes; the exact caching is left to the implementation.

Group heartbeats. The group coordinator adds the token and, when needed, the list to successful ConsumerGroupHeartbeat, ShareGroupHeartbeat and StreamsGroupHeartbeat responses at version N or later:

  • The token is always set on such a response.
  • The list is set when the request's token is -1 or differs from the current token, and is null otherwise.
  • Responses with a top-level error, and responses to a member leaving the group, carry no group configuration information: token -1 and a null list. Such a response does not change the client's cache; the client clears its cache as part of its own explicit departure handling (see Client).

Share fetch and acknowledge. The share partition leader handling a ShareFetch or ShareAcknowledge request at version N or later does the same with the share configurations it applies, using its own snapshot for the group. The values describe that broker's local state; different leaders can report different values while their bounds or defaults differ, for example during a rolling change.

Timing. A value describes the configuration as resolved when the broker built the response. The snapshot guarantees two things: that the list, the token and any existing field carrying the same value are consistent with each other, and that they describe the configuration as resolved at that time. It does not guarantee that work already in progress used that snapshot. Session timeout changes are picked up when the coordinator next schedules or refreshes the member's session timer, so the reported value does not describe the remaining lifetime of an already scheduled timer; a new record lock duration applies to locks acquired or renewed afterwards, not to locks already held; an assignment in progress is not recomputed. Changing the handling of the request itself to a snapshot-based model is out of scope.

Client

The Java consumer, share consumer and Kafka Streams clients support the new fields. Their behavior does not change: they keep using the existing fields (heartbeat interval, task offset interval, acceptable recovery lag, acquisition lock timeout) as today. The new list is used only for logging.

Cache. A client keeps the token together with the list it identifies, per key: one key for the group heartbeat, and one key per broker for the share fetch and acknowledge path, shared by ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge. It sends the token of the key it is talking to, or -1 if it holds none.

The heartbeat token, list and deduplication state are maintained for the same group within a client instance and are cleared when the client explicitly leaves the group or closes. Coordinator rediscovery and automatic rejoining after fencing or an unknown-member error do not clear this state. Explicit departure includes unsubscribe(), where supported. The client clears the cached state as part of the local departure handling, independently of whether the leave request succeeds. A subsequent subscription and rejoin are treated as a fresh observation for logging. A leave sent because the poll interval expired is not an explicit departure: the state is kept, and the following rejoin is not a fresh observation.

On the share path the client discards the token, list and deduplication state for a broker when it discards its local share session state for that broker: when it closes the session because no partitions remain on that broker, when the broker is no longer in the cluster metadata, or when the client closes. Re-establishing a session after SHARE_SESSION_NOT_FOUND, INVALID_SHARE_SESSION_EPOCH, SHARE_SESSION_LIMIT_REACHED or a connection error keeps the state, and the first request of the new session carries the held token. Partition leadership moving away does not by itself discard the state. A session established after the local state was discarded is treated as a fresh observation.

  • A response with a list replaces the list and the token of that key.
  • A response with a valid token and no list confirms the client's state only if the request carried the token that the client still holds for that key. Otherwise the client resets the token of that key to -1, so that the next request asks for the full list.
  • A response with token -1 leaves the cache unchanged.
  • Losing or clearing the list resets the token to -1.

Logging. The client follows the rules under Client logging in Public Interfaces: the cache and the deduplication state are per key and share the lifetime described above. Configuration names the client does not know are logged in the same way.

Other clients may ignore the new fields; tagged fields they do not understand are skipped, as required by the protocol since KIP-482.

Compatibility, Deprecation, and Migration Plan

The change is backward compatible in both directions. Nothing is deprecated and no migration is needed.

  • New client, old broker. The negotiated version is below N, so the client sends no token and receives no list. It behaves as today and logs nothing new.
  • Old client, new broker. The request is below N, so the broker does not include the new fields, since they are defined only from version N.
  • New client, new broker. The client receives the list on the first successful response and whenever the reported state changes.
  • Mixed broker versions, for example during a rolling upgrade. Share partition leaders on different versions may or may not include the list. A client only logs what it receives, keyed by broker, and deduplicates logs per broker according to the cache lifetime rules above.
  • Coordinator changes and token generation. A new coordinator with the same content and the same token generation produces the same token, and the client keeps its list without receiving it again. Changes to the token-generation algorithm between releases may cause additional full-list responses, for example on each move between coordinators that generate tokens differently, but do not change client behavior or trigger duplicate logs when the reported contents are unchanged.
  • Non-Java clients. The new fields are tagged, so clients that do not implement this KIP skip them, as required since KIP-482.
  • Release coordination. KIP-1313 introduces a new version of every RPC in Apache Kafka 4.5. If this KIP is implemented in the same release, the fields are added to those versions in coordination with KAFKA-20925; otherwise this KIP adds the next version of the five RPCs.

No configuration changes. Clients that do not want the new log lines can adjust the log level of the logger concerned, as for any other log message.

Test Plan

Unit tests:

  • Resolution. For each configuration, the reported Value equals the value the broker uses for its behavior: with and without a group override, with a clamped override in each direction, with a dynamically clamped broker default, and with an unavailable Streams task assignor.
  • ConfiguredValue. It is set for a clamped override and for the assignor fallback, and null otherwise, including for an override equal in value but different in text (for example "060000"), and for a clamped broker default.
  • Rendering. Integers, booleans, strings, lists in configured order, empty strings and empty lists are rendered as specified.
  • Snapshot and token. All entries, the token and the existing fields in one response come from the same state. The distinct snapshots used in the tests produce distinct tokens, the same content produces the same token on different brokers, and -1 is never issued.
  • Heartbeat responses. The token is set on successful responses at version N. The list is set for token -1 or a different token, and null for the current token. Responses with an error and responses to a leaving member carry token -1 and a null list. Requests below version N get neither field.
  • Share responses. ShareFetch and ShareAcknowledge carry the leader's own state, and two leaders with different bounds report different values.
  • Client cache. A list replaces the cache. A null list is accepted only when the request carried the currently held token, and otherwise resets the token. Token -1 leaves the cache unchanged. Share keys are kept per broker.
  • Client logging.
    • INFO is logged once per content per key and again after the content changed and changed back.
    • A list received with a new token but unchanged content logs nothing.
    • The same mismatch reported by two share partition leaders is warned about once per broker.
    • A different effective value for the same configuration is warned about separately.
    • A mismatch that is resolved for a key and reappears is warned about again.
    • A leave response logs nothing and changes nothing.
  • Cache lifetime and failover.
    • Coordinator change with the same content and the same token generation: the client sends its token and receives no list.
    • Coordinator change with the same content but a different token: the client receives the full list, replaces the token, and logs nothing.
    • After UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID or FENCED_MEMBER_EPOCH, automatic rejoining retains the cached state. Unchanged contents produce no duplicate logs; changed contents update the cache and are logged according to the per-key rules.
    • Explicit leave, including unsubscribe() and a leave whose request fails, clears the heartbeat state; a subsequent rejoin logs the list again and warns again about a remaining mismatch.
    • A leave caused by an expired poll interval keeps the heartbeat state; the automatic rejoin logs nothing when the contents are unchanged.
    • Re-establishing a share session with the same broker after SHARE_SESSION_NOT_FOUND or a connection error keeps the state; the first request of the new session carries the held token and logs nothing when the contents are unchanged.
    • Share partition leadership moves: the old broker's key is discarded when its local share session state is discarded. The new leader is a fresh observation only if the client does not already retain state for that broker; otherwise its existing cache and deduplication state are reused and nothing is logged for unchanged contents.
    • A broker restarts with changed bounds: the client holding the old token receives the full list and warns about the new mismatch.
    • A response carrying a list is lost: the client's next request carries its old token and receives the full list again.
  • Authorization. A client with the permissions the RPC already requires, but without DESCRIBE_CONFIGS, receives the list. A response with a top-level GROUP_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED error carries token -1 and no list. A ShareFetch response with a partition-level TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED error still carries the token and, when due, the list.
